title: Hi, I’m Your New Press Secretary, and It’s My First Time Reading Words Out Loud
excerpt: I’m your new press secretary, Katie Zacharia! You may know me from my appearances on Fox News; I am pretty sure that is how the president knows me
body: I’m your new press secretary, Katie Zacharia! You may know me from my appearances on Fox News; I am pretty sure that is how the president knows me
That is how he identifies all possible candidates for jobs: turning on the TV and pointing
I also might be a lawyer! Where did I pass the bar, you ask? After I moved to China

No further questions! (See, I am getting into the press-secretary spirit already.) When you consider that this is my first time reading words out loud, today was actually a pretty impressive performance
I swear that I have seen a sentence before, and I know where one stops and
With a rising inflection? This lends an air of trepidation to every one of my prepared words, as though saying any one of them aloud might cause a trapdoor to open beneath me
I’m bringing a kind of “unlicensed bus driver” energy to this speech: unsteady at best, with many seemingly random stops in unexpected places
Just call me Vote by Mail, because my delivery is raising a lot of questions in the White House

I am excited for this job because—well, let me use my exact words: “I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply, and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people

And what I hope to do in this position is to take that into an official capacity and only build on, only amplify, and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins he’s making for Americans, for, for Americans to understand how much has changed in this brief period of time—what he’s been able to accomplish
My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson and will absolutely be leading the way as with that.” So there you have it
Wasn’t it Dan Quayle who once said that “verbosity leads to unclear, inarticulate things”? I assume he meant that positively! Am I enjoying this job? In a word: no
I thought there would be more saying “HOW DARE YOU” to people asking questions, which I felt equipped to do
By the way, how do you think this is going so far? I have referred to my husband as “my president” only one time! That’s good, right? Let me preempt some of your questions for me
No, I am not what turns up when you Google woman who has just seen the letters of the alphabet for the first time and is frightened of all of them
Did you see me drink water even a single time? Yes, I am the best person for the job, provided the job does not involve reading any more words or answering any more questions
This is the kind of meritocracy we’ve come to expect from the Trump administration
As Pete Hegseth and I like to say, it’s not meritocracy if it doesn’t include me
No further questions! And look at that—it’s been 14 whole minutes already
That’s time! Good thing I will never have to do this again.

title: A Novel That Turns the Tables on AI
excerpt: What’s the point of playing? Games don’t provide an organism with food, water, or shelter
body: What’s the point of playing? Games don’t provide an organism with food, water, or shelter
They distract from the pursuit of survival and reproduction

And yet play is found across the animal kingdom; the act separates creative, joyful, living creatures from “merely mechanical things,” as the Dutch historian and cultural theorist Johan Huizinga once put it

In his famous 1938 study on games and play, Homo Ludens , Huizinga asserts that the behavior represents something fundamentally absurd: Humans “play and know that we play, so we must be more than merely rational beings, for play is irrational.” Huizinga’s analytical understanding of leisure remains influential in the fields of philosophy and game design
Perhaps this is why the British writer Joanna Kavenna, halfway through her zany, cerebral romp of a novel, Seven , quotes at length from Huizinga
Play is necessary, she quotes him as saying, even if “we live in a demented world.” Humans aren’t robots, Kavenna seems to be reminding us

And her novel, which lands during a moment when the biggest question about robots is whether they’ll kill us all, offers a jaunty insight: When we embrace our irrationality, we deepen our understanding of what separates us from our computers

The plot and thematic structure of Seven are guided by an invented board game, Seven, which resembles chess and involves a spiral-shaped board known as the “box.” The game involves seven movable pieces and two six-sided dice, and its rules are flexible; the novel itself is punctuated by four separate sets of instructions. (This slipperiness will become important later on.) In the same way that chess has been used by writers and artists as a metaphor for war or existential struggle, Seven becomes a symbol for how humans attempt to make sense of their world’s incoherence
Kavenna’s characters are deadly serious about their game, but the author is willing to poke fun at them
The action begins in a university philosophy department in Oslo, where the nameless, genderless narrator works as a research assistant to an Icelandic philosopher named Alda Jónsdóttir

The professor’s area of study is called “box philosophy,” and it focuses on the problem of “Thinking Outside the Box About Thinking Outside the Box.” What does the assistant’s job look like in practice? They spend time getting too drunk at faculty dinner parties, doing menial work for Jónsdóttir, and “asking questions,” but their first matter of serious business is “working on none of the above.” They try to clarify: “I don’t mean that I didn’t work on anything I’ve just mentioned, but that I worked on the category of None of the Above .” This deadpan joke serves a narrative function, priming the assistant—and the reader—to start thinking beyond the rules, and to enter a more expansive realm. [ Read: Open AI just carpet-bombed mathematics ] Jónsdóttir sends the narrator away on, essentially, a wild-goose chase to Greece; their mission is to hunt down a man named Theódoros Apostolakis—a poet, dentist, and Seven enthusiast who is “big in boxes.” This journey across Europe includes several professional Seven competitions, during which the rules keep changing
Everything the assistant learned in Norway seems useless except the central lesson—to think outside the box
These games abroad lead the narrator to start contemplating the role of recreation, the limits of human ingenuity, and the meaning of consciousness

Soon this will bring them face-to-face with the novel’s ultimate threat, an artificial-intelligence program that undermines everything that Jónsdóttir and the Seven players care about: creativity, curiosity, play. “How do you play a game without rules?” Kavenna writes. “Do you just make stuff up and hope for the best?” These thoughts coalesce in the second half of the novel, when an AI bot named the Quail is introduced

Invented by a Seven player named Indrek Laar, who, Kavenna pointedly notes, believes that “AI was very clever and therefore had experiences,” the Quail is named for qualia , a term borrowed from philosophy. (It’s meant to capture a quality of consciousness, though the narrator dismisses it as “a baroque way of saying ‘experience.’”) The bot is “designed to play Seven” and nothing else, Kavenna writes. “It couldn’t give you relationship advice or sympathise when you were feeling sad, or translate the Iliad or write your homework
It just played Seven.” And it does its job well

The Quail manages to beat the world’s reigning Seven champion, Ashok Deo, in a humiliating match that the narrator calls both the “greatest Seven game of the millennium” and “the worst game ever”—technically impressive, but absolutely demoralizing. “No one had enjoyed it,” Kavenna writes, “because the Quail couldn’t experience enjoyment and the Quail’s proxy—Indrek Laar—was horrified.” Ashok’s loss echoes real-life incidents in which computers have won games against humans, such as the 1997 victory of IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer over the chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov and the repeated defeats of the Go champion Lee Sedol by Google’s program AlphaGo in 2016
Culturally, these results represented a significant shift in how we understand the relationship between humans and computers
The Kasparov match “had the impact of a Greek tragedy ,” one audience member told The New York Times
But its reception wasn’t all bad: Another champion commented, “Nice style!” while watching Deep Blue take another round
The machine, she admitted to the Times , “made many moves that were based on understanding chess, on feeling the position

We all thought computers couldn’t do that.” Deep Blue, and AlphaGo after it, seemed to do more than just win by brute force: They encroached on the human flair for creativity. [ Read: Yet another literary prizewinner seems to be AI ] Those machines—and the fears they inspired—can look quaint when compared with today’s technology
Some AI-safety researchers see it as an existential threat to humankind
Earlier this year, an OpenAI model not meant to have open access to the internet managed to break out of its “sandbox” and hack the databases of another tech company, Hugging Face
Cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated and more prevalent
AI-company employees are publicly quitting , raising alarms about the safety culture inside major firms

Popular conversations are inundated by pessimism—and at the same time, companies are advertising their services by urging onlookers to “stop hiring humans,” as in one controversial San Francisco– and New York–based billboard campaign
The stakes of the conflict between human and computer capabilities can feel bleak and funereal
Kavenna’s portrayal of the battle of man versus machine is leavened, however, by her sense of humor

Machines may be able to beat us, but has a computer ever written an effective joke? Beyond being funny, the novel also defies machines by eschewing binaries (“I was neither one thing nor another,” the genderless, nameless, race-less narrator observes of their mental state. “I was mostly in a state of / .”) But Kavenna’s pitch for human superiority really comes together in the novel’s denouement
Eventually, the narrator meets a Seven champion named Eleni Hikaru Jones
She’ll point out that when Deep Blue beat Kasparov, the latter “carried on playing the game

He accepted that Deep Blue was better than him, but he was still the best human player.” This idea inspires the characters to one-up machine intelligence by changing the rules of the game—or, in Kavenna’s framing, thinking outside the box
While Ashok plays the Quail, Indrek, the bot’s inventor, recognizes the turmoil he’s unleashed
Human loneliness, not malice, was his motive: “He made the Quail so he would always have someone to play with.” Knowing this, Eleni persuades Indrek to join forces with her
Together, they cook up a scheme to create an AI bot that can beat the Quail, and call it the Red Fox

As these two AIs spend an evening rapidly moving through Seven matches against each other, the humans find better things to do: In the time it takes Eleni and Ashok to play a single leisurely game of Seven, the Red Fox beats the Quail 147 times
But the new device hasn’t accomplished anything of value to either person
In the end, a human Seven champion does indeed beat the Red Fox—but not by winning a Seven match

Instead, she accomplishes something like breaking out of her sandbox: Although Eleni “hadn’t won the game, she had won the game,” the narrator tells us cryptically, as though reciting a riddle or koan

title: Trump’s Affection for Russia Is No Mystery
excerpt: A large majority of the Republican Party, including many officials who initially viewed Donald Trump with deep skepticism, decided early in Trump’s first term t
body: A large majority of the Republican Party, including many officials who initially viewed Donald Trump with deep skepticism, decided early in Trump’s first term that the investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 election were the hysterical product of Trump Derangement Syndrome in the Deep State and the media
There was no mystery to solve, no scandal to uncover, in Trump’s affinity for Vladimir Putin
And yet this strange alliance continues to bedevil American foreign policy

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced that he had held another call with Putin, and came away once again depicting the Russian dictator as a cherished friend to whom he owes a great deal. “I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” he wrote on Truth Social
Later that day, Trump reemphasized his debt of gratitude. “I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you
We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel, which is what we want
So, thank you,” he told reporters outside the White House. [ Read: Why is Kash Patel planning to visit Russia? ] Many of Trump’s comments make little sense, and these were no exception
But he was using a particular kind of illogic that conflicts with his standard brand of nonsense
Trump typically depicts international trade in starkly mercantilist terms
Exports, in his mind, are a form of profit, and imports are a loss
Trump sees trade deficits as a form of theft, and conceives of a “good deal” as one in which the United States reduces its imports or increases its exports
This holds true of all goods, including oil. “We don’t need their fuel, we don’t need their energy, we don’t need their oil and gas
We don’t need anything that they have,” Trump said dismissively of Canada last year
Yet when it comes to imports from Russia, Trump inverts his standard accounting methods

He presents Russian oil as a kind of gift, something Putin plans to “supply.” (A more accurate verb to describe this transaction would be sell .) In reality, diesel fuel exists in a global market, and adding a small amount of Russian diesel into this enormous international supply would have a barely detectable effect upon its price
A more important effect would be on the Russian economy
Economic sanctions have hampered its ability to attract foreign currency, and the Trump-Putin plan would suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports
Doing so would in fact appear to violate American law, which prohibits importing oil from Russia unless it makes peace with Ukraine, though illegality does not usually deter Trump
The most immediate outcome of this plan has been to present Ukraine as the cause of economic turmoil and Russia as the innocent victim of Ukrainian warmongering
Trump almost immediately began to praise Putin and assail the Russian dictator’s adversary
Volodymyr Zelensky “could have settled this war many times—many, many times—and he chooses not to,” Trump told reporters on Friday outside the White House. “He wants to make problems for the world

He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel, because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.” Trump’s solution? “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal
Because they could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does.” There is no universally agreed-upon explanation for why Trump has remained so consistently faithful to Putin
One theory holds that Putin masterfully strokes Trump’s ego
Although Trump does respond to flattery, the flaw in this hypothesis is that other leaders have tried, and often failed, to mimic this formula
Europeans have met Trump’s second term with obsequious displays and gifts
Ukraine floated a proposal to rename the Donbas region “Donnyland.” Poland proposed christening a base “Fort Trump.” Yet these countries have remained largely frustrated
A second theory holds that Trump simply admires dictators
This one contains a bit more truth, as seen by Trump’s swooning over Xi Jinping and even Kim Jong Un
But the dictators running Iran and Venezuela have hardly managed to duplicate the Trump-Putin partnership
A third theory depicts Trump as merely amoral, driven by transactions and indifferent to moral concerns
Yet he has continued to defer to Putin even as the Russian dictator has undermined Trump’s own standing by aiding Iran in its war with the United States
Meanwhile, Zelensky’s assistance against Iran seems to have bought him no goodwill whatsoever

Trump’s view of the war is moralistic—he simply blames the victim rather than the aggressor. “You don’t start a war against someone 20 times your size and then hope that people give you some missiles,” he said last year of Zelensky
Explaining the depth of Trump’s identification with Putin may require looking at a possibility that conservatives have been dismissing out of hand for a decade: manipulation and corruption
During the 2016 campaign, Russia dangled a lucrative deal to develop Trump-branded properties in Russia that would deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in profit with no risk
More recently, The New York Times reported that Trump advisers and Russian officials have floated deals that would enrich Trump’s inner circle as part of ending the war
Russia has tried to bribe foreign officials, especially by handing out pieces of its resource wealth, in numerous countries

It would be strange if Putin didn’t try to replicate this tried-and-true method in the United States. [ Anne Applebaum: Trump’s message to Ukraine is now crystal clear ] Perhaps the best evidence against corruption is that Trump now has access to so many other sources of wealth that he hardly needs any financial incentive to tilt toward Russia
Yet Putin seems able to bring the American president around to his way of thinking, if not effortlessly (their most recent phone call reportedly consumed an hour and a half) then at least reliably

title: Trump’s Dubious Claim About the Ilhan Omar Search
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Donald Trump is the quantum president: simultaneously all-powerful and also a wee, innocent figurehead, blithely unaware of what his aides are doing

The first Trump, the one who declares that he “alone can fix it,” was in the Oval Office last week, asserting his unfettered power to persecute his political opponents. “I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton
I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden

I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama,” he said. “I can do whatever I want, if I want.” But after federal law enforcement conducted a search at the Washington, D.C., home of Representative Ilhan Omar, the Minnesota Democrat, yesterday morning, Trump insisted he was completely uninvolved
Without more information, the search—conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations, a division of ICE that handles complicated probes—is deeply troubling

The Trump administration has deployed a series of probes, searches, and indictments, many of which are plainly pretextual or political, against outspoken critics. (This is a crucial distinction from an August 2022 search at Mar-a-Lago, which yielded many boxes of highly sensitive material, haphazardly stored.) Black women, including Representative LaMonica McIver of New Jersey, New York Attorney General Letitia James , and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook , have been particular but not exclusive targets
The search also breaks a norm against public action in highly political cases in the 60 days before an election
Attempts to intimidate or criminalize an opposition party are hallmarks of authoritarianism

There is much about the search that we do not know, including what evidence was used to obtain the warrant (though The New York Times reports it “was the subject of significant back and forth between prosecutors and the federal judge who eventually approved it”); what agents might have found; and what charges, if any, the government might be contemplating

Some reporting states that prosecutors are exploring whether Omar’s late father lied or made omissions on immigration applications. (The administration has focused on trying to strip citizenship from people who gave false responses on applications.) The congresswoman came to the United States as a child and became a naturalized citizen at 17

To hear Trump tell it, he also knows little about the probe. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said yesterday. “I have nothing to do with it.” (The Department of Justice told the Times that the search was part of an ongoing investigation but declined to comment further.) This is a pattern I previously identified : When faced with difficult questions or strong pushback, the president tends to insist that the lawyers are in charge and he’s not apprised of what’s going on
Trump has repeatedly said that he has a “right” to direct federal prosecutors to investigate whomever he wishes, and although he generally insists that he has not done so, evidence suggests otherwise

Last September, Trump posted on Truth Social instructing then–Attorney General Pam Bondi to take action against critics, including James, former FBI Director James Comey, and Senator Adam Schiff. “We can’t delay any longer, it’s killing our reputation and credibility
They impeached me twice, and indicted me (5 times!), OVER NOTHING
Several news outlets later reported that the missive was intended as a private message
Bondi was removed this spring, reportedly because of Trump’s frustration that his attempts at retribution were moving too slowly

In February, FBI agents searched an election center in Fulton County, Georgia, in pursuit of evidence for Trump’s assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. (Their warrant was largely based on debunked claims .) The following day, Trump spoke directly to some of the agents involved, an extraordinary intervention

Comey was ultimately charged with threatening the president, after he posted a photograph of shells he found on a beach that read 86 47 , a set of numbers that supporters have said connotes wanting to remove Trump from office
DOJ has insisted the post was a threat of violence (which Comey has denied)
Documents released by Comey’s lawyers this summer show that Trump was closely involved in the case, demanding briefings and notes from interviews with Comey prior to his indictment

Adding to the impression that the Omar case is a White House effort, Katie Miller, the former Trump aide and the wife of Stephen Miller, posted about the story on X yesterday, saying, “Promise made, promise kept.” She later deleted the post
But even if Trump is not personally engaged, he has made clear through his statements that he wants Omar investigated and punished

In 2019, he suggested that members of the progressive “Squad,” which included Omar, should “go back and help fix the totally broken and crime infested places from which they came.” A few days later, after he criticized Omar at a rally, he watched as a crowd chanted, “Send her back!” In December, he called Omar “garbage” and said that Somalis should leave the U.S: “Their country stinks, and we don’t want them in our country.” The next month, when Omar was attacked at an event, Trump accused her of setting it up

This March, Vice President Vance told an interviewer, “We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud.” The message from the White House is clear enough to make King Henry II blush
If Trump is as engaged in prosecutions of his political opponents as public evidence indicates, then his behavior is inappropriate and damaging to the rule of law
If, however, he truly knows nothing about what’s going on, then he’s not the heroic, powerful leader he claims to be
Which would he prefer the public conclude? Related: Trump is hiding behind his lawyers

title: What If AI Is the End of the World?
excerpt: Our sense that life is meaningful depends, perhaps more than we realize, on our confidence that humanity will go on after we die
body: Our sense that life is meaningful depends, perhaps more than we realize, on our confidence that humanity will go on after we die
If we came to believe that humanity had no future, the philosopher Samuel Scheffler argues , much of what we value would lose its meaning or motivating force
What would follow would be widespread “apathy, anomie and despair.” That is one reason why the threat of artificial intelligence feels so different and disorienting
When some of the most knowledgeable people within an industry suggest that their work could, within a matter of years, lead to global catastrophe and even human extinction, it’s decidedly unnerving
AI-driven anxiety is now showing up in therapy offices across the country
Much of what has given people succor in the past—faith that there are good things and good people who will outlive us, and that the story will go on—feels like it might be suddenly removed
Consider the dread, even the paralyzing fear, you might feel if you were told as you prepared to fly that your plane has a 1-in-100 chance of crashing, or perhaps even a 1-in-10 chance
Even worse, if the plane you boarded did crash, it would be a terrible, localized tragedy
But the world would go on; your children would outlive you
Some of the primary architects of AI, though, are talking about the permanent end of the human species
Perhaps they are wrong; other experts are less concerned with AI destroying humanity than with it being unreliable, misused, or recklessly deployed

Their warnings, though, are hard to ignore. [ Juliette Kayyem: Destroying humanity is against the law ] It is better that we name the fear honestly rather than avoid it: All of us may soon perish, and everything we have made may go with us
Then we need to separate the urgent practical questions—what do we do to prevent the worst from happening?—from the existential

How should we live in light of the possibility, however remote, of the end of all that we have known and loved and has ever been? As the focus on the existential threats posed by AI increases, people will exhibit a range of responses

Robert Jay Lifton coined the term psychic numbing to describe what he saw among survivors of Hiroshima: a protective shutdown of emotional responses in the face of catastrophic events or potentially overwhelming trauma
There can also be denial—a sense that the prospects are so awful that they can’t be true, and even if they are, there’s nothing we can individually do about it
Still others are tempted toward “information avoidance,” in which we ignore information because we’re afraid of an unpleasant outcome
Some set the threat aside as best as they can, a bit like avoiding a visit to a doctor out of fear that the physician will confirm a serious, even life-threatening illness
Still others drift toward a nihilism that ends in despair
When the future itself seems in doubt, the long-term commitments that sustain a meaningful life can start to seem pointless
My own reaction has been to search for footholds of reasonable hope
I’ve looked to knowledgeable voices for reassurance
I don’t have certainty that things will turn out just fine, but I want to believe that there are promising paths forward and what we do still matters
I should acknowledge, too, that the idea of an extinction-level threat doesn’t yet fully register with me
Because nothing like this has ever happened before, my instinctive assumption is that it never will
But it would be foolhardy not to contemplate the possibility
Viktor Frankl found meaning in life amid the horror of Auschwitz
Though we cannot control external events, he believed, we can retain control over our interior world
We choose how we respond to circumstances we did not create, to cups we would prefer to let pass
This “tragic optimism” is the capacity to say yes to life despite enormous suffering
Meaning can be chiseled even out of anguish
The impermanence of things is no reason for despair; instead, it increases the urgency to make meaning of the time we have, the moments in which we live, and the things we choose to love
The question is always what life is asking of us in every situation we face

And the answer is that life asks us to live lives of integrity, honor, and devotion to things and people outside of ourselves, to celebrate truth and beauty even in dark times. “A thought transfixed me,” Frankl wrote, in Man’s Search for Meaning . “For the first time in my life I saw the truth as it is set into song by so many poets, proclaimed as the final wisdom by so many thinkers
The truth—that love is the ultimate and the highest goal to which man can aspire
Then I grasped the meaning of the greatest secret that human poetry and human thought and belief have to impart: The salvation of man is through love and in love

I understood how a man who has nothing left in this world still may know bliss, be it only for a brief moment, in the contemplation of his beloved.” He added, “For the first time in my life I was able to understand the meaning of the words, ‘The angels are lost in the perpetual contemplation of an infinite glory.’” Meaning is found not only in what we accomplish but also in beholding what we love
ALBERT CAMUS’ 1947 NOVEL, THE PLAGUE , is a tale of horror, survival, and resilience in the face of a devastating epidemic
The story’s protagonist, Bernard Rieux, is a dedicated, resolute physician in the Algerian city of Oran
He embodies what Jean Tarrou, a visitor who organizes volunteer sanitary squads, calls a “true healer.” Rieux fights the plague day after day, with no expectation of winning

title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
excerpt: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next
body: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next
Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk
The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify

Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach

But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information

Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly
But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization
Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth
What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics
A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API
An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available

Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development
But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one
Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives
They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research
When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses
But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering
They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models
Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla
And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure

But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have

In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like

The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses
If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it

Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea

Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands

He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations

Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models

There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic , several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit
Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks
When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts
But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model
There are other important lines of defense
AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no

title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
excerpt: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few y
body: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old
But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money

He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups

Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged
Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April
Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents
Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models
Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026
CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales
Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business
Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools

Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets
Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs
Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls
Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear
No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives

Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening

This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records
And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups

Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too
But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans
He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls
The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees

To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations
Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it
Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer
Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first
Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

title: Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs
url:
<title>Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765586/original/file-20261012-60-88eirj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3800%2C2533&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Increasing Social Security benefits annually helps millions of older Americans afford necessities.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/vero-beach-florida-publix-grocery-store-supermarket-female-news-photo/2268676973?phrase=older%20person%20paying%20in%20a%20store&amp;adppopup=true">Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The nearly <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/quickfacts/stat_snapshot/">76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits</a> are slated to find out on Oct. 14, 2026, how much their monthly check will rise. This <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/latestCOLA.html">cost-of-living adjustment</a>, or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities.</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://umaine.edu/directory/ums_directory/pankaj-agrrawal-2/">finance professor</a>, and one of the topics I research is how <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5013829">inflation affects retirees’ investment choices</a>. And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face.</p>

<p>The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual <a href="https://www.bls.gov/cpi/">inflation rate as of September 2026</a>, which the  Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, will also release on Oct. 14. It <a href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/cpi.pdf">stood at 3.4% in August</a>, according to the BLS. Experts have no doubt that the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be far above the <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html">2.8% for 2026</a> and <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2025.html">2.5% for 2025</a>. Many forecasts <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/11/business/economy/social-security-cola.html">range from 3.4% to 3.6%</a>.</p>

<p>But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured.</p>

<p><iframe id="kbm52" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/kbm52/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A column chart with columns ranging from 0 to 14.3% for the years 1975-2025."></iframe></p>

<h2>Calculating the COLA</h2>

<p>The government has <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/ssb/v67n3/v67n3p73.html">annually increased Social Security benefits</a> to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices.</p>

<p>The metric that the government uses is its <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/oact/STATS/cpiw.html">consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers</a>, known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index.</p>

<p>The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January. </p>

<p>If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, <a href="https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/colaseries.html">benefits stay the same</a>. That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015. </p>



<h2>Spending much of the bump on premiums</h2>

<p>One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation.</p>

<p>Out-of-pocket health costs, including <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs">Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments</a> for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan <a href="https://crr.bc.edu/retirees-are-worried-about-the-cost-of-healthcare-and-who-can-blame-them/">Center for Retirement Research at Boston College</a>.</p>

<p>For example, the government deducts <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/publications/11579-medicare-costs.pdf">Medicare Part B premiums</a> directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The <a href="https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/2026-medicare-parts-b-premiums-deductibles">standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90</a> in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA.</p>

<p>More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/medicare-basics/working-past-65">most Americans getting Social Security benefits are</a>, helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation.</p>

<p><iframe id="meHCU" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/meHCU/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A split-bar chart showing that Social Security benefit increases are growing in real terms to a lesser degree than the costs of Medicare Part B premiums."></iframe></p>

<h2>Finding other options</h2>

<p>Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the <a href="https://seniorsleague.org/cola-watch/">Senior Citizens League</a> and the <a href="https://www.ncpssm.org/documents/social-security-policy-papers/the-cpi-e-a-better-option-for-calculating-social-security-colas/">National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare</a>, say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs. </p>

<p>There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the <a href="https://www.bls.gov/cpi/research-series/r-cpi-e-home.htm">consumer price index for Americans 62 and older</a>, known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12675">some efforts in Congress</a> to make the switch.</p>

<p>The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older <a href="https://www.ncpssm.org/documents/social-security-policy-papers/the-cpi-e-a-better-option-for-calculating-social-security-colas/">spend more than twice as much</a> as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates.</p>

<p>Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W. </p>

<p>But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has <a href="https://crr.bc.edu/what-is-the-right-price-index-for-the-social-security-cola/">increased less than CPI-W in some years</a>. What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293688/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation

Finding other options Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees
Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs
There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate

The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch
The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care
People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates
Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014
It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W
But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment
The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years
What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose

<title>Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece – adding to the global vacancies sapping US embassies</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765933/original/file-20261013-50-5g3am7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C216%2C5677%2C3784&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio unveil a plaque at the Greek foreign ministry in Athens on Oct. 7, 2026.

</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/ambassador-to-greece-kimberly-guilfoyle-and-us-secretary-of-news-photo/2298426455?phrase=guilfoyle%20greece&amp;adppopup=true">Mark Schiefelbein/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The United States is down one more ambassador. On Oct. 13, 2026, it emerged that President Donald Trump had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, a MAGA loyalist and ex-fiancée of Trump’s son Donald Jr., to <a href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-ambassador-greece-guilfoyle-9da9d2e50e18bccc38946404c1ca756f">resign her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece</a>, a NATO ally. It follows allegations that the Trump adviser turned diplomat pushed for a Republican donor to <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/guilfoyle-amex-donor-100-000-0e02cdc3">pay off her six-figure American Express bill</a>.</p>

<p>Guilfoyle later confirmed that she would comply with the request <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/us/politics/kimberly-guilfoyle-resign.html">and resigned</a>. In so doing, Athens became one of a number of U.S. overseas missions with a vacancy at the top. In fact, <a href="https://afsa.org/list-ambassadorial-appointments">93 out of 196 U.S. ambassador jobs</a> are currently unfilled.</p>

<p>And that is after <a href="https://www.senate.gov/pagelayout/legislative/one_item_and_teasers/nom_confc.htm">U.S. senators confirmed 10 new ambassadors</a> before leaving town on Sept. 30, 2026. Among those nodded through before Congress closed for an extended midterm recess were new U.S. ambassadors for Kenya, Nicaragua, Malaysia and Kyrgyzstan.</p>

<p>With some of the vacancies the White House has not even sent names to Capitol Hill, despite the second Trump administration being a year and a half into the job. With others, the Senate, which is controlled by the same party as the White House, hasn’t acted on the names put forward. Should the Athens position be added to the list, the reason will be down to potential insufficient vetting or an ill-advised appointing strategy that promotes loyalty over experience.</p>

<p>Regardless of the reason, as a <a href="https://sites.tufts.edu/murrowcenter/leadership/">former ambassador and an expert in the process of diplomacy</a>, I find the current vacancies concerning. Among those embassies still without a top person in place are key partners for the U.S. – countries that Washington needs to achieve its security, economic and strategic objectives. </p>

<p>What makes these vacancies more worrying, in my view, is that they come amid other concerning developments in the State Department’s staffing of embassies. </p>

<h2>Politicizing diplomacy</h2>

<p>Chief among them are the <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/08/06/trump-fills-ambassador-posts-with-more-donors-loyalists-than-any-recent-president/">high percentage of politically appointed ambassadors</a> relative to positions filled by career diplomats – that is, senior foreign service officers, usually with at least 20 years of diplomatic experience.</p>

<p>Though many countries send politicians abroad as ambassadors, America’s diplomatic service is unique in two ways. The percentage of U.S. ambassadors who are political appointees – those who haven’t followed a career civil service path – is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiae116">higher than comparative countries</a> across the world. Second, those political appointees are <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-insistence-on-personal-loyalty-from-ambassadors-could-crimp-us-foreign-policy-273087">often donors with little to no government experience</a>.</p>

<p>The practice has existed for decades, but in recent years the <a href="https://afsa.org/appointments-barack-obama">number of political appointees has increased</a>. During the Obama administration, the percentage of political appointees was around 30%. The number rose to around 40% in the first Trump administration and the subsequent Biden administration.</p>

<p>But in Trump’s second term, some <a href="https://afsa.org/appointments-donald-j-trump-2nd-term">80% of names the White House has sent</a> to the Senate have been political.</p>

<p><iframe id="mMPO8" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/mMPO8/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="bar chart of career vs. political ambassadors."></iframe></p>

<p>And many of the people Trump has put forward don’t appear to have the credentials usually associated with holding important diplomatic positions. Rather, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/08/06/trump-fills-ambassador-posts-with-more-donors-loyalists-than-any-recent-president/">many are friends, associates or donors</a> to Trump, often with little overseas experience or knowledge of the country they are going to. </p>

<p>Lee Lipton, <a href="https://ph.usembassy.gov/ambassador-lee-lipton/">ambassador to a key ally in the Philippines</a>, is owner of a restaurant in Palm Beach – Florida  Benny’s on the Beach – a member of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club and a contributor to his political campaign.</p>

<p>The system of political appointees has always had an element of handing ambassadorships to friends and supporters. But what has changed under Trump is the range of positions now available. In the past, ambassadors to key countries like Chile, Israel, Peru, the Philippines, Turkey and Egypt, for example, have almost always been career appointees. This has changed under the second Trump administration.</p>

<p>Appointing noncareer diplomats to small, faraway nations has the additional problem that the chosen individual may not actually spend much time there. The rule of thumb has long been that ambassadors should spend no more than one month every year back in the United States. But that is compromised if a noncareer diplomat with expansive business ties in the U.S. is selected.</p>

<h2>The role of a deputy</h2>

<p>A closely related problem is the State Department’s handling of an ambassador’s second in command, their <a href="https://afsa.org/current-deputy-chiefs-mission">deputy chiefs of missions</a> – DCMs for short – under Secretary of State Marco Rubio.</p>

<p>During Trump’s first term in the White House, politically appointed ambassadors were often <a href="https://theconversation.com/trumps-insistence-on-personal-loyalty-from-ambassadors-could-crimp-us-foreign-policy-273087">encouraged to swap out the DCMs</a> they inherited from their predecessors. It meant going through a long hiring process, leaving those key jobs unfilled for months. </p>

<p>In 2025, the State Department went further, canceling the assignments of senior officers <a href="https://www.nbcwashington.com/news/national-international/trump-removes-nearly-30-career-diplomats-from-ambassadorial-positions/4032589/">en route to take up embassy jobs</a> and opening a new hiring process.</p>

<p>It formed part of a Trump purge of what many MAGA Republicans <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/dec/23/trump-administration-recalls-30-ambassadors-promote-loyal-diplomats">characterized as a “deep state” civil service</a>. The reality is that DCMs <a href="https://diplomaticacademy.us/2024/12/29/advice-for-political-ambassadors/">fill a critically important role</a> in helping political appointees navigate the bureaucracy and implement their policy ideas, as well as raising the occasional reality check.</p>

<p>With more politically appointed ambassadors – some of them with no relevant experience – having an experienced DCM can be the difference between success and failure.</p>

<h2>Looking for other friends</h2>

<p>When you put all of these personnel changes together, the result is the degradation of what was once seen as one of the most effective diplomatic services in the world.</p>

<p>What makes this potentially more worrying is where the vacancies are. For example, Belarus and Bulgaria, neighbors to Russia and Ukraine, are without U.S. ambassadors. And important countries in the fight against terrorism or in geopolitical hot spots, such as Kuwait, Qatar and Mauritania, are in the same camp.</p>

<p>Other countries still without ambassadors include Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s largest nation and the most populous Muslim-majority country in the world; key Middle East ally Egypt and nuclear power Pakistan; and nations the U.S. needs to help manage inward migration, such us Haiti and Guatemala.</p>

<p><iframe id="rMRg2" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rMRg2/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map shows countries without U.S. ambassadors"></iframe></p>

<p>The problem of absent or inexperienced ambassadors goes both ways. It means Washington may not have a capable diplomatic figurehead in these countries to contact in times of need. There are also fewer avenues for host nations to successfully convey messages back to the U.S. administration.</p>

<p>When faced with absent ambassadors, amateurish political appointees and deputy mission chiefs who are very junior or career appointees with short resumes, host countries may conclude that they aren’t seen as important to the U.S. and start looking elsewhere for friends.</p>

<p>And the U.S. has hollowed out its ambassadorial corps at a time when it is facing growing international influence by the <a href="https://www.rand.org/nsrd/projects/russian-arms-sales-and-sanctions-compliance.html">likes of Russia</a>, <a href="https://www.usglc.org/chinas-growing-influence-is-america-getting-left-behind/">China</a> and Iran – rival nations hoping to capitalize on a perceived diplomatic void left by Washington.</p>

<p>For example, as the U.S. tries to <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/a-framework-for-u-s-policy-toward-china-2/">contain Beijing’s influence</a> in the Asia-Pacific region, Fiji, Indonesia and Laos remain without U.S. ambassadors. Similarly, China’s diplomatic relations with Pakistan – a former key security partner for Washington – have grown while the ambassadorial seat in Islamabad remains empty.</p>

<p>And former Soviet states including Georgia and Kazakhstan don’t have U.S. ambassadors even as Russia President Vladimir Putin attempts to consolidate Moscow’s regional influence.</p>

<p>In large areas of the world, such as Africa and the Pacific region, and in important areas of policy, the lights may be on in U.S. embassies, but nobody’s home. And that is a distinct problem for national security and strategic interests.</p>

<p><em><em>This is an updated version of an <a href="https://theconversation.com/missing-ambassadors-inexperienced-appointees-is-washington-dropping-the-diplomatic-ball-293487?notice=Article+has+been+updated.">article originally published</a> on Oct. 7, 2026.</em></em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294315/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: I’ve been studying election integrity for 26 years, and here’s why I expect a normal election this November instead of chaos
