<title>I’ve been studying election integrity for 26 years, and here’s why I expect a normal election this November instead of chaos</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765595/original/file-20261012-60-xhqha1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Concern about election interference by the Trump administration sparked this rally in Washington, D.C., on Sept, 15, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-participants-and-signage-during-the-hands-off-our-news-photo/2295431041">Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for People&#39;s Action Institute</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><em>Fear of <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/06/16/nx-s1-5702491/trump-voting-threat-midterm-election-dhs">federal interference in the 2026 midterms</a>, from intimidation stoked by armed officials at the polls to seizure of ballots, has been growing in the United States. That’s led state and local voting officials across the country to <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/national/2026/09/24/midterm-2026-election-preparation-federal-interference/">draw up plans for scenarios</a> requiring them to summon law enforcement or prepare legal filings <a href="https://www.governing.com/politics/election-officials-prepare-for-federal-intervention-in-the-midterms">so they can keep the polls open</a>.</em></p>

<p><em>In an interview with The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor Naomi Schalit, <a href="https://www.lls.edu/faculty/justinlevitt/">election law scholar Justin Levitt</a> takes the temperature down a bit. Levitt says that while voting officials’ preparations mean they are doing their jobs, the anticipated election interference won’t happen – in part because of that preparation.</em></p>

<p><strong>Schalit: Could we see widespread intimidation and challenging of voters at the polls?</strong></p>

<p>Levitt: It’s extremely unlikely. I completely understand that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5946736/voting-confusion-turnout?">Americans are freaked out</a>. They are at an electric level of anxiety right now, not just about the world but about the coming elections. But I don’t think the intimidation and challenges they’re fearing or forecasting are going to manifest for a couple reasons.</p>

<p>I have <a href="https://www.laloyolan.com/news/loyola-law-professor-justin-levitt-appointed-senior-advisor-for-president-biden/article_4fbb98fe-d785-5737-9483-0b4048affabb.html">run a nationwide election protection program</a>. It’s real work to get people to dedicate a full day to helping others. It’s that much harder to recruit a group of people to show up and look for fraud, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/us-elections-donald-trump-voting-fraud-db0a438023d8451c2854940504b48547">and fraud at scale doesn’t really happen</a>. It’s even harder to recruit people to show up to actively intimidate voters. </p>

<p>Not that many people are in for it – there are keyboard warriors who love to act out online, but to actually show up is a totally different thing. And they’re really risking either getting thrown out of the polling place or going to jail, <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/594">because intimidating voters is a crime</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C243%2C4662%2C2622&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man leaning over a table where quite a few people sit, with a sign 'Vote HERE' next to the table." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C243%2C4662%2C2622&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765445/original/file-20261011-50-f6dqep.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Residents check in to vote in the primary at a polling place at Morgan Elementary School on Aug. 4, 2026, in Shelby, Mich.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/residents-vote-at-a-polling-place-inside-the-gymnasium-at-news-photo/2289061687?phrase=signing%20in%20voters&amp;adppopup=true">Scott Olson/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>What about intimidation and challenges by government officials?</strong></p>

<p>On the government side, which is something people are also really freaked out about, we are a giant country and there are <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/polling-places">almost 100,000 polling places</a>. The logistics of an intimidation operation don’t work countrywide. </p>

<p>To go from Step A, I’d like to intimidate people, to Step C, intimidate people everywhere? You’re missing a pretty giant Step B. </p>

<p>Here’s what I believe will happen: The federal government will send a group of a dozen goons to a suburban polling place somewhere, and they’ll have a camera crew with them. Bystanders will happily oblige them in filming. That clip will go viral and scare voters into not showing up at the polls because they think that there are individuals intimidating voters all over the place.</p>

<p>If people are worried about intimidation, go outside and see for yourself that in your neighborhood things are very normal. Even if social media depicts pure chaos.</p>

<p><strong>Local and state election officials are preparing for <a href="https://www.votebeat.org/national/2026/09/24/midterm-2026-election-preparation-federal-interference/">mayhem or interference by the federal government</a>. Are their efforts just based on overwrought imaginations?</strong></p>

<p>No, they are being responsible. It’s their responsibility to prepare for everything so that the voters don’t have to worry about it. And they are as prepared as I have ever seen them. <a href="https://www.governing.com/politics/election-officials-prepare-for-federal-intervention-in-the-midterms">They’re preparing for a lot of truly outlandish scenarios</a>, and some that are more realistic, so that they can be ready to make sure that the election is smooth and secure and feels very normal.
</p>

<p><strong>Could ballots be seized by state or federal officials?</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.wgcu.org/2026-09-09/ballot-seizures-seemed-impossible-but-judges-and-officials-are-prepping-for-them-now">Ballot seizure is also very much on people’s minds</a>, and I think it’s particularly salient because <a href="https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/09/what-the-fulton-county-election-warehouse-raid-did-and-did-not-accomplish/">the feds did it in Fulton County, Georgia</a>, and because local sheriffs did it in Riverside, California. But there are two big reasons that’s not going to happen this fall. </p>

<p>First, the seizures in both Fulton County and Riverside were of old ballots. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/04/us/politics/fulton-county-fbi-raid-trump-gabbard.html">Fulton County’s ballots were 6 years old</a>. California was more recent. <a href="https://statecourtreport.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/california-supreme-court-finds-sheriffs-seizure-650000-ballots-unlawful">It was a 2026 seizure for the 2025 elections</a>, but those elections were still over and results had already been tallied. </p>

<p>That’s very different from <a href="https://electionlawblog.org/wp-content/uploads/berstein-seizure.pdf">an attempt to seize ballots while results are still pending</a>, <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/legal-guardrails-against-rubber-stamping-search-warrants-elections">which is flatly unconstitutional</a>. I just <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7227158">worked on an article</a> with the former chief of the public integrity section at the U.S. Department of Justice. We did a lot of research and we think there’s never before been a <a href="https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/search-warrants-for-election-materials-get-their-day-in-court">federal warrant to seize ballot material</a> when the results are pending. And that’s because judges don’t like to sign off on things that are illegal.</p>

<p>These seizures, in Fulton County and in Riverside, California, surely took the judges in those districts by surprise. Judges see applications for search warrants all the time, all day, every day. But <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/legal-guardrails-against-rubber-stamping-search-warrants-elections">warrants for election materials</a> when the results are still pending are vanishingly rare. The warrants in Fulton and Riverside did us a favor because there are very few judges anywhere who are going to be surprised right now. <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/democrats-sue-doj-over-midterm-ballot-seizure-plans/">Those seizures were big news</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ym4YLiKogwU">In Fulton County, the judge allowed it</a>, but he said very, very clearly <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.gand.355452/gov.uscourts.gand.355452.108.0_1.pdf#page=42">this would be different</a> if we were talking about a pending election where results weren’t still in the door. <a href="https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/04/chad-bianco-election-warrants/">In California, the trial judge signed off on it</a>. But the California Supreme Court came back just about a month ago, <a href="https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/09/supreme-court-ruling-sheriff-ballot-seizure/">said this was absolutely, flatly illegal</a>, there is absolutely no reason why a sheriff needs to seize these ballots. It is unlawful under California state law in a way that mimics other states’ laws too. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7PNr8PXmrwA?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon discusses the state’s concerns about voter intimidation.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><strong>If somehow ballots get seized during the election process before they are counted and certified, that would mean that the chain of custody was broken and they would no longer be valid. Is that correct?</strong></p>

<p>In the extraordinarily unlikely event that there’s actually a seizure, we’re in a little bit of terra incognita. It’s not entirely clear what happens. There will be immediate efforts legally to get the ballots back. </p>

<p>But the <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/elections-q-and-a-for-lawmakers">election system is built with belts and suspenders</a>. If there’s a seizure of some materials, that doesn’t mean there’s a seizure of all materials or all materials relevant to a count. Sometimes there are paper ballots that are <a href="https://verifiedvoting.org/verifier/#mode/navigate/map/voteEquip/mapType/ppEquip/year/2026">backed up by electronic copies</a>, or vice versa. So what’s really important is that the election officials have a set of reliable records they can count.</p>

<p>The federal government may come in and say, “Give us the materials,” and the states are likely to say, “How about we make you copies?” And that’s fine. They can go off and have their copies and do whatever they want with them as long as the states are still able to count the records. It’s not really clear what would happen if there’s an extended lapse where the ballots are out of state custody. It’s not that those ballots are immediately invalid, but there’d be a fight about it. </p>

<p><strong>I’ve been covering politics for a long time, and in the past 10 years the number of times we’ve gone into terra incognita was entirely unanticipated. Which is why I have to ask certain questions that seem completely implausible.</strong></p>

<p>I’ve been working on elections for a couple decades now. My list of things to watch out for in 2000 was long. My list of things to watch out for in every subsequent election grew longer. The last couple of years, my list of things to watch out for has spilled off the page and onto the floor. For election officials, it’s a lot. They are stressed out, they’re underpaid, they’re overworked. </p>

<p>But all that said, they’ve got this. They’re actually as prepared as I have ever seen, including dealing with things that they haven’t ever seen before and should never have to be seeing. </p>

<p>I understand why people are afraid. I understand why people think there are risks. And that’s because it’s not normal to have the president fostering this much concern about the democratic process and who is this unattached to the democratic process.</p>

<p>But the good news is <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-trump-cant-just-decree-changes-to-voting-by-mail-a-former-federal-judge-explains-how-the-presidents-executive-order-is-a-solution-looking-for-a-problem-280680">the process doesn’t depend on the president</a>. It depends on us.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294094/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for People's Action Institute Fear of federal interference in the 2026 midterms , from intimidation stoked by armed officials at the polls to seizure of ballots, has been growing in the United States
That’s led state and local voting officials across the country to draw up plans for scenarios requiring them to summon law enforcement or prepare legal filings so they can keep the polls open
In an interview with The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor Naomi Schalit, election law scholar Justin Levitt takes the temperature down a bit
Levitt says that while voting officials’ preparations mean they are doing their jobs, the anticipated election interference won’t happen – in part because of that preparation
Schalit: Could we see widespread intimidation and challenging of voters at the polls? Levitt: It’s extremely unlikely
I completely understand that Americans are freaked out
They are at an electric level of anxiety right now, not just about the world but about the coming elections
But I don’t think the intimidation and challenges they’re fearing or forecasting are going to manifest for a couple reasons
I have run a nationwide election protection program
It’s real work to get people to dedicate a full day to helping others
It’s that much harder to recruit a group of people to show up and look for fraud, and fraud at scale doesn’t really happen
It’s even harder to recruit people to show up to actively intimidate voters
Not that many people are in for it – there are keyboard warriors who love to act out online, but to actually show up is a totally different thing
And they’re really risking either getting thrown out of the polling place or going to jail, because intimidating voters is a crime
Residents check in to vote in the primary at a polling place at Morgan Elementary School on Aug. 4, 2026, in Shelby, Mich

The logistics of an intimidation operation don’t work countrywide

Here’s what I believe will happen: The federal government will send a group of a dozen goons to a suburban polling place somewhere, and they’ll have a camera crew with them
Bystanders will happily oblige them in filming
That clip will go viral and scare voters into not showing up at the polls because they think that there are individuals intimidating voters all over the place
If people are worried about intimidation, go outside and see for yourself that in your neighborhood things are very normal
Local and state election officials are preparing for mayhem or interference by the federal government
Are their efforts just based on overwrought imaginations? No, they are being responsible
It’s their responsibility to prepare for everything so that the voters don’t have to worry about it
And they are as prepared as I have ever seen them
They’re preparing for a lot of truly outlandish scenarios , and some that are more realistic, so that they can be ready to make sure that the election is smooth and secure and feels very normal

Could ballots be seized by state or federal officials? Ballot seizure is also very much on people’s minds , and I think it’s particularly salient because the feds did it in Fulton County, Georgia , and because local sheriffs did it in Riverside, California
But there are two big reasons that’s not going to happen this fall
First, the seizures in both Fulton County and Riverside were of old ballots
It was a 2026 seizure for the 2025 elections , but those elections were still over and results had already been tallied

<title>More rehab centers should mean fewer overdoses. In one California region, we found the opposite</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756873/original/file-20260830-50-ugvevp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5138%2C3425&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">In Orange County, Calif., an area dense with treatment centers, out-of-state patients overdose in greater numbers than elsewhere in the state. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/blurred-motion-shot-of-speeding-ambulance-royalty-free-image/482184235?phrase=ambulance%20orange%20county&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Manuel Sulzer/Connect Images via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At 24, Boyd was living in Chicago when he decided to get help. He had been drinking alcohol since a young age, but more recently he’d been drinking far more often – and dangerously.  </p>

<p>He found a rehabilitation center online and reached out to the facility in Orange County, an affluent coastal area of Southern California, for treatment.</p>

<p>Boyd, a pseudonym used at his mother’s request, checked in at the facility, where he completed his initial detox and participated in therapy sessions. He was later readmitted to the same rehab program twice after his initial intake, his mother told the coroner’s office of the Orange County Sheriff’s Department.</p>

<p>Eventually he was moved to another nearby location operated by the same treatment program. However, despite the stated policy of sobriety on the treatment program’s website, Boyd began to use fentanyl.</p>

<p>In June 2024, two weeks after his final readmission, Boyd was found unresponsive in the bathroom at that facility, according to the coroner’s report.</p>

<p>He arrived at the emergency room in cardiac arrest; his heartbeat was restored, but he had minimal brain function, the coroner’s report later found. He remained on life support and died six days later.</p>

<p>The coroner’s office ruled his death an accidental fentanyl overdose. </p>

<p>Boyd’s story is not an isolated one. It points to a larger problem in the treatment industry. We are psychologists who research societal factors that contribute to overdoses. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10826084.2026.2634978">Our recent study</a> found that out-of-state residents overdose in excessive numbers in Orange County, a hub for addiction treatment centers, compared with the rest of the state. </p>

<p>This finding runs counter to previous research that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2021.102579">consistently shows</a> that areas with more treatment facilities tend to have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2021.109143">fewer</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2014.12.008">overdoses</a>.</p>

<h2>Exploiting addiction and insurance fraud</h2>

<p>In response to the opioid crisis in the United States, federal laws <a href="https://doi.org/10.1215/03616878-2416325">now require</a> most private health insurance plans to cover addiction treatment. These laws have been mostly beneficial, <a href="https://journalofhealthcarefinance.com/index.php/johcf/article/view/240">providing millions of Americans access</a> to treatment they otherwise could not afford. </p>

<p>However, the large amounts of insurance money flowing into the treatment industry have also attracted dishonest operators <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2017/07/07/opioid-insurance-fraud">looking to score easy profits</a>, especially in areas with weak regulatory oversight of treatment facilities.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://downloads.asam.org/sitefinity-production-blobs/docs/default-source/public-policy-statements/final-pps-on-government-strategies-to-foster-ethical-addiction-treatment.pdf">common scheme is to recruit</a> patients with generous insurance plans to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/forefront.20180423.449595">enroll at treatment centers</a>, then <a href="https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2015/07/31/addiction-treatment-bonanza-how-urine/6891814007">bill their insurance companies</a> for unnecessary or poor-quality services at inflated prices. <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4024397">These reimbursement</a> <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/south-florida-addiction-treatment-facility-operators-convicted-112-million-addiction">payments</a> can allow owners to <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2017/06/16/addiction-treatment-the-new-gold-rush-its-almost-chic">pocket enormous sums of money</a>, from a few hundred to <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/18540861/united-states-v-17654800-in-us-currency/">US$3,000 per day</a> for each patient.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/feature/megyn-kelly/florida-s-billion-dollar-drug-treatment-industry-plagued-overdoses-fraud-n773376">These schemes</a> are <a href="https://www.pbcms.org/assets/PBC%20Opioid%20Crisis_PBC%20Response.pdf">most profitable</a> when patients have out-of-network private insurance, which tends to have higher spending limits.</p>

<p>Even the most generous insurance plans cover treatment for a limited time, <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2017/05/28/addict-brokers-opioids">perhaps a few weeks</a> to a <a href="https://time.com/4950199/affordable-care-act-opioid-relapse">few months</a>. Once that coverage runs out though, a <a href="https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/catferguson/addiction-marketplace">patient who relapses can be readmitted</a> to treatment, and the expensive insurance billing cycle <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2019/10/21/my-years-in-the-florida-shuffle-of-drug-addiction">can begin</a> again.</p>

<p>This creates a perverse financial <a href="https://www.congress.gov/115/crec/2018/06/12/CREC-2018-06-12.pdf">incentive</a> for unethical operators to provide substandard care – or even interfere with recovery. <a href="https://www.congress.gov/event/115th-congress/house-event/106716/text">Numerous</a> <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2017/05/21/how-some-southern-california-drug-rehab-centers-exploit-addiction">investigations</a> <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3666389">have documented</a> how patients can become trapped in a revolving door of treatment, relapse and reenrollment, with each relapse putting them at risk of overdose and death. </p>

<h2>Far from a local problem</h2>

<p>Some patients travel outside their home state to receive treatment, and unscrupulous rehab operators <a href="http://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-023-10217-z">often recruit</a> such patients.</p>

<p>Their websites <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2017/05/21/how-some-southern-california-drug-rehab-centers-exploit-addiction">promise</a> expert care and feature photos of luxurious accommodations. Prospective patients are sometimes <a href="https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/local/2016/10/30/patient-brokering-festering-wound-for/6992696007">given</a> free one-way plane tickets, along with free housing and living expenses. There is even a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-023-10217-z">market</a> of third-party patient <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/29767342241279194">recruiters</a> – or patient brokers – who get large <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.josat.2024.209609">kickbacks</a> from treatment centers for each patient they bring to the facility.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="An aerial photo with palm trees, buildings, water and mountains at sunset." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=337&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758036/original/file-20260904-50-s3cqga.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An aerial view of Orange County, Calif., home to an area with a large concentration of addiction treatment facilities.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/anaheim-skyline-royalty-free-image/1281007272?phrase=anaheim%20regional%20medical%20center&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Matt Gush/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Even when patients arriving from other states do not already have private insurance, they can <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4024397">purchase</a> a California insurance policy as soon as they arrive. Patient <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-023-10217-z">brokers sometimes</a> arrange this coverage and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.josat.2024.209609">pay</a> the insurance costs on the patient’s behalf. </p>

<p>People who travel long distances for treatment are particularly vulnerable to exploitation. Before arriving, they have little opportunity to see the actual conditions of the facility. Once they arrive, they are separated from their support network of family and friends back home, making them even more dependent on the facility.</p>

<p>When a patient’s insurance coverage comes to an end, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/us-news/drug-rehabs-insurance-curbing-6c56ded6">they can be kicked out</a> regardless of whether <a href="https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/catferguson/addiction-marketplace">they’ve recovered</a>. Patients who are far from home may not be able to afford the return trip. In some cases, they may face a <a href="https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/11/25/especially-disgusting-former-workers-patients-level-accusations-at-addiction-treatment-empire/">difficult choice between</a> homelessness or relapsing in order to stay in the treatment system that at least provides them with a place to live.</p>

<h2>A hot spot of treatment facilities</h2>

<p>Orange County, California, has <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2023/07/06/california-to-audit-its-regulation-of-addiction-treatment-facilities">a large concentration</a> of addiction treatment programs and has <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2021/12/16/dept-of-justice-orange-county-is-now-nations-center-for-addiction-fraud">long been identified</a> as a <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-series-cases-combat-addiction-treatment-kickback-schemes">major center</a> of treatment-related fraud. </p>

<p>California’s oversight of the addiction-treatment industry has been <a href="https://sd34.senate.ca.gov/news/senator-umberg-reintroduces-substance-use-disorder-treatment-reform-measure">frequently criticized</a> <a href="https://www.ocregister.com/2024/11/10/addicts-came-to-southern-california-from-afar-to-get-sober-they-wound-up-dead">as</a> <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4024397">inadequate</a>, and the unusually large number of treatment facilities in Orange County makes misconduct even harder to detect.   </p>

<p>According to 2019 federal data, there were 14 treatment centers per 100,000 residents in Orange County, compared with 5 per 100,000 <a href="https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt29389/2019_NSSATS/2019_NSSATS.html">residents</a> <a href="https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2021/2020-census-apportionment-results.html">nationwide</a>.  </p>

<p>One question we had was whether the large addiction treatment industry might contribute to more drug overdoses in the area. We reasoned that even if only a small fraction of treatment programs exploit patients, a larger industry would give rise to more of these programs – and potentially more overdoses.</p>

<p>We identified a 10-city region in Orange County with the highest number of rehab facilities, which had 35 treatment centers per 100,000 residents. We call this the study area. </p>

<p>We then compared overdose cases treated at the eight emergency departments in the study area with overdose cases treated at all of California’s other emergency departments. </p>

<p>Our analysis examined over 33 million visits to 323 hospitals throughout California from 2019 through 2021, the most recent data available when we began the study. To protect patient identities and comply with our data-sharing agreement, we can’t name the cities or hospitals in the study area. </p>

<h2>Excessive overdoses</h2>

<p>To determine whether overdoses were unusually high or low, we compared them with bodily injuries, which is one of the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhamcs/web_tables/2022-nhamcs-ed-web-tables.pdf">most common reasons</a> for treatment at an emergency department. In other words, bodily injuries served as a benchmark for the overall number of emergency department cases seen in the area. This approach can be useful when population sizes, such as the total population of visitors to the study area, are unknown.</p>

<p>Specifically, we compared the relative frequency of overdoses and injuries in the study area with the rest of California. A larger share of overdose cases in the study area would suggest overdoses were disproportionately high there. </p>

<p>We also identified how far people were from their homes when treated at the emergency department. We looked at three groups: Californians treated in their home counties, Californians who were outside their home counties, and out-of-state residents who were visiting California.</p>

<p>The differences were striking.</p>

<p><iframe id="JMNyf" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/JMNyf/3/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Percent difference in overdose-to-injury ratio ER visits by patient residency: Orange County study area, 2019-21"></iframe></p>

<p>Emergency patients who lived in the study area were treated for 4,108 overdoses. Relative to injuries, overdoses were 10% higher than expected when compared with patients who lived in other parts of California. However, this effect was dwarfed by what we observed in the other two groups.</p>

<p>California residents who visited the study area were treated for 370 overdoses. Again, relative to injuries, overdoses were 68% higher than expected when compared to Californians who visited other parts of the state. </p>

<p>Finally, out-of-state visitors to the study area were treated for 316 overdoses. Here, overdoses were a staggering 159% higher than expected relative to out-of-state visitors to the rest of California. </p>

<p>One possible explanation is that the region’s many treatment centers simply attracted more visitors who are already struggling with addiction and thus more susceptible to overdose. We suspect there is some truth to this. However, we do not think it accounts for the more than twofold difference we observed between in-state and out-of-state visitors.</p>

<p>We believe this difference is at least partially the result of out-of-state visitors put at risk by predatory treatment schemes in Orange County, and especially in the study area.</p>

<h2>Gaps in oversight</h2>

<p>Weak oversight has allowed these predatory schemes to persist in California. </p>

<p>The California Department of Health Care Services, the state agency that licenses and oversees addiction treatment centers, has been criticized as having <a href="https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/01/14/reform-for-californias-fraud-plagued-addiction-treatment-in-2026/">lax regulations</a> governing how most private-pay rehabs can operate.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.auditor.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2023-120-Report.pdf">agency is also slow</a> to investigate complaints, taking an average of nearly a year to complete most investigations and about three months to do so after a patient dies at a treatment center, according to an audit by the state.</p>

<p>In an email to The Conversation, a DHCS spokesperson said the audit covered fiscal years 2020-21 through 2022-23, “a period significantly affected by pandemic-related delays,” and that improvements to its investigation processes were already underway. The agency “proactively assigned staff to Orange County to address the region’s high volume of complaints and ensure timely investigations,” the spokesperson said.</p>

<p>A facility’s license can be revoked or suspended for extreme violations, but even in these cases its owner can continue to operate other rehab centers under a different company name and resume the same predatory practices there.</p>

<p>Although our research focused on one area in California, treatment fraud has also been occurring at <a href="https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2025/01/15/florida-addiction-treatment-promise-dcf-fails-to-show-oversight/76942298007">rehab centers across</a> <a href="https://ncnewsline.com/briefs/lawmakers-advocates-launch-initiative-targeting-predatory-practices-in-addiction-treatment">the</a> <a href="https://www.mcdermottlaw.com/insights/new-jersey-expands-patient-brokering-statute-to-include-laboratories-recovery-homes">United</a> <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/kentucky-addiction-recovery-care-medicaid-fraud">States</a>, especially in places with looser oversight of the treatment industry. Many follow a similar pattern and target people from outside the local area.</p>

<p>One important takeaway for people considering treatment, and for their families, is to be very cautious about traveling far from home to enter a facility you have never seen in person. </p>

<p>Besides causing real harm to vulnerable patients and their families, these schemes also <a href="https://whyy.org/segments/drug-rehab-as-money-game">undermine people’s</a> <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-115hhrg28931/pdf/CHRG-115hhrg28931.pdf">trust</a> in legitimate treatment providers and drain vast sums of money from the healthcare system – <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/health-industry/calif-bill-targets-profiteering-in-addiction-treatment-dialysis-industries">costs</a> that are passed on to insured patients and taxpayers.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/285569/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: In Orange County, Calif., an area dense with treatment centers, out-of-state patients overdose in greater numbers than elsewhere in the state
Manuel Sulzer/Connect Images via Getty Images At 24, Boyd was living in Chicago when he decided to get help
He had been drinking alcohol since a young age, but more recently he’d been drinking far more often – and dangerously
He found a rehabilitation center online and reached out to the facility in Orange County, an affluent coastal area of Southern California, for treatment
Boyd, a pseudonym used at his mother’s request, checked in at the facility, where he completed his initial detox and participated in therapy sessions
He was later readmitted to the same rehab program twice after his initial intake, his mother told the coroner’s office of the Orange County Sheriff’s Department
Eventually he was moved to another nearby location operated by the same treatment program
However, despite the stated policy of sobriety on the treatment program’s website, Boyd began to use fentanyl
In June 2024, two weeks after his final readmission, Boyd was found unresponsive in the bathroom at that facility, according to the coroner’s report
He arrived at the emergency room in cardiac arrest; his heartbeat was restored, but he had minimal brain function, the coroner’s report later found
He remained on life support and died six days later
The coroner’s office ruled his death an accidental fentanyl overdose
It points to a larger problem in the treatment industry
We are psychologists who research societal factors that contribute to overdoses
Our recent study found that out-of-state residents overdose in excessive numbers in Orange County, a hub for addiction treatment centers, compared with the rest of the state
This finding runs counter to previous research that consistently shows that areas with more treatment facilities tend to have fewer overdoses
Exploiting addiction and insurance fraud In response to the opioid crisis in the United States, federal laws now require most private health insurance plans to cover addiction treatment
These laws have been mostly beneficial, providing millions of Americans access to treatment they otherwise could not afford

However, the large amounts of insurance money flowing into the treatment industry have also attracted dishonest operators looking to score easy profits , especially in areas with weak regulatory oversight of treatment facilities
A common scheme is to recruit patients with generous insurance plans to enroll at treatment centers , then bill their insurance companies for unnecessary or poor-quality services at inflated prices
These reimbursement payments can allow owners to pocket enormous sums of money , from a few hundred to US$3,000 per day for each patient
These schemes are most profitable when patients have out-of-network private insurance, which tends to have higher spending limits
Even the most generous insurance plans cover treatment for a limited time, perhaps a few weeks to a few months
Once that coverage runs out though, a patient who relapses can be readmitted to treatment, and the expensive insurance billing cycle can begin again
This creates a perverse financial incentive for unethical operators to provide substandard care – or even interfere with recovery
Numerous investigations have documented how patients can become trapped in a revolving door of treatment, relapse and reenrollment, with each relapse putting them at risk of overdose and death
Far from a local problem Some patients travel outside their home state to receive treatment, and unscrupulous rehab operators often recruit such patients
Their websites promise expert care and feature photos of luxurious accommodations
Prospective patients are sometimes given free one-way plane tickets, along with free housing and living expenses
There is even a market of third-party patient recruiters – or patient brokers – who get large kickbacks from treatment centers for each patient they bring to the facility
An aerial view of Orange County, Calif., home to an area with a large concentration of addiction treatment facilities
Matt Gush/iStock via Getty Images Even when patients arriving from other states do not already have private insurance, they can purchase a California insurance policy as soon as they arrive
Patient brokers sometimes arrange this coverage and pay the insurance costs on the patient’s behalf
People who travel long distances for treatment are particularly vulnerable to exploitation
Before arriving, they have little opportunity to see the actual conditions of the facility
Once they arrive, they are separated from their support network of family and friends back home, making them even more dependent on the facility
When a patient’s insurance coverage comes to an end, they can be kicked out regardless of whether they’ve recovered
Patients who are far from home may not be able to afford the return trip
In some cases, they may face a difficult choice between homelessness or relapsing in order to stay in the treatment system that at least provides them with a place to live
A hot spot of treatment facilities Orange County, California, has a large concentration of addiction treatment programs and has long been identified as a major center of treatment-related fraud

title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?

<title>Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765699/original/file-20261012-60-vkn69w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2142%2C3228%2C2152&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Shoppers are much more inclined to buy misshapen produce if they can be assured the quality is good.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/red-and-green-bell-pepper-VM5Yj2GrSOQ">Carly Reeves on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/10/08/cost-concerns-dominate-as-publics-economic-ratings-turn-more-negative/">Almost three-quarters</a> say they’re feeling stressed out about <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/consumers/grocery-price-inflation-customer-reactions-346487f7">skyrocketing grocery bills</a>. But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early.</p>

<p>Overall, the U.S. government estimates that <a href="https://www.usda.gov/about-food/food-safety/food-loss-and-waste/food-waste-faqs">30% to 40% of all food</a> – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing <a href="https://theconversation.com/fewer-americans-are-getting-help-buying-groceries-from-snap-benefits-as-states-grapple-with-the-programs-cascade-of-changes-292829">food insecurity</a>, but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, <a href="https://unfccc.int/news/food-loss-and-waste-account-for-8-10-of-annual-global-greenhouse-gas-emissions-cost-usd-1-trillion">8%-10% of carbon emissions</a> globally result from food waste. </p>

<p>In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/foods-funny-looking-future-ugly-produce-delivery-11557343181">marketing “ugly” produce</a> to appeal to more consumers to <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-food-industry-looks-to-turn-garbage-to-gold-11570662300">upcycling food by-products</a>. </p>

<p>I study <a href="https://www.binghamton.edu/som/research/profile.html?id=jzhang157">how consumers evaluate product value</a> and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242920988656">many shoppers assume</a> that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better. </p>

<p>What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first. </p>

<h2>Making ‘ugly’ food attractive</h2>

<p>A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like <a href="https://indyweek.com/sponsored/featured/hungry-harvest-provides-food-box-subscriptions-with-purpose/">Hungry Harvest</a> and <a href="https://blog.misfitsmarket.com/misfits-market-2025-year-in-review/">Misfits Market</a> are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint.
Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="The photo image depicts a misshapen tomato, pepper, strawberry, lemon, ginger root and carrot." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=76%2C0%2C1847%2C1039&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765697/original/file-20261012-50-sew1np.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Companies that sell ‘misfit’ produce have seen a surge of consumer interest in recent years.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Jintao Zhang</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Another example is <a href="https://www.thepacker.com/news/sustainability/how-food-waste-apps-are-reshaping-grocery-retail">Too Good To Go</a>, an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/too-good-to-go-and-whole-foods-market-add-seven-new-surprise-bag-offerings-expanding-food-saving-efforts-nationwide-302612424.html">530 Whole Foods stores</a>. And the app <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/90849958/flashfood-food-insecurity-grocery-store-waste">Flashfood</a> encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals. </p>

<p>Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a <a href="https://www.thepacker.com/news/sustainability/how-food-waste-apps-are-reshaping-grocery-retail">67% jump from the year before</a>, while Misfits Market rescued <a href="https://blog.misfitsmarket.com/misfits-market-2025-year-in-review/">27 million pounds of food</a> (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from <a href="https://blog.misfitsmarket.com/misfits-market-2021-annual-report/">23 million</a> (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its <a href="https://blog.misfitsmarket.com/what-a-year-its-been-our-2019-recap/">first full year</a> of operation.</p>

<p>This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242920988656">tend to judge misshapen produce</a> as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242918816319">Another study</a> found 
that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “<a href="https://business.columbia.edu/research-brief/ugly-produce-food-waste-bias">Different Outside. Same Inside</a>” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food.</p>

<h2>The upcycling boom</h2>

<p>This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from <a href="https://www.earthday.org/press-release/barnana-snacks-and-earthday-org-announce-earth-month-partnership/">rescued bananas</a>. </p>

<p>Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through <a href="https://www.wherefoodcomesfrom.com/upcycled">Upcycled Certified</a> if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than <a href="https://www.preparedfoods.com/articles/131208-upcycled-food-movement-gains-scale-credibility-and-global-momentum-in-2025">600 products</a> from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products <a href="https://www.producemarketguide.com/news/upcycled-certified-products-rise-17-year-over-year">grew 17%</a> from 2024 to 2025. </p>

<p>Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/cb.1844">they made their purchase decision</a> based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart. </p>

<p>But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this <a href="https://www.stockupexpress.com/collections/baking-desserts/products/renewal-mill-upcycled-okara-flour">small bag of specialty flour</a> going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers.</p>

<p>Generational attitudes differ on this point, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/cb.1844">our research found</a>. Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality.</p>

<p>That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store. </p>

<p>A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms.</p>

<h2>When logos matter</h2>

<p>The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10454446.2021.1955798">simple logo</a> could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucv049">higher quality</a>, while descriptive ones <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0022243719845000">lift brand evaluations</a>. The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A logo for upcycled foods notes it was established in 2019 and urges shoppers to 'stop food waste.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765591/original/file-20261012-50-at4006.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Shoppers respond more favorably to logos that provide information and incentives, research has found.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">From Jintao Zhang.</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference. </p>

<p>It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there.</p>

<p>Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. The rescue economy can make that case, but it has to lead with quality and not only with conscience.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293526/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Today’s irreverent politics ignore ancient wisdom: The need to know your limits</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765340/original/file-20261010-50-rt0nx1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C485%2C3051%2C2033&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">For Plato, a key political virtue was reverence: the virtue governing shame, as well as awe.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ribera-Platon-Amiens.jpg">Jusepe de Ribera/Musée de Picardie via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2025/04/21/thirsty-awards-congress-annual-list-00267374">common complaint today</a> laments the “<a href="https://www.idahostatesman.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article270777667.html">shamelessness” of politicians</a>. Until recently, the argument goes, more elected officials had <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/pages/shameless">a sense of shame</a> to hold them back from ugly words and deeds, at least in public. Many in the current crop, however, seem to have <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/pages/shameless">no fear of disgrace</a>; they <a href="https://thehill.com/opinion/campaign/3472449-shameless-politicians-reflect-a-shameless-society/">revel in contempt</a> for the niceties of old – unwritten rules against cursing, slander or lying, but also written rules against <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/713933/record-high-say-government-corruption-widespread.aspx">abuse of power</a>. </p>

<p>The problem isn’t so much a question of bad manners or even of corruption. It’s really about leadership.</p>

<p><a href="https://umaine.edu/directory/ums_directory/robert-a-ballingall/">I study the history of political thought</a> and work on the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-31303-5">psychology of lawfulness</a>: the character traits citizens need for the rule of law to work. One such trait is each person’s ability to limit herself – to revere some larger principle that she would be ashamed to betray.</p>

<p>That’s all the more true for good leaders, even in a constitutional republic <a href="https://theconversation.com/3-ways-trump-is-acting-like-a-king-and-bypassing-the-constitutions-checks-and-balances-on-presidential-authority-249347">defined by checks and balances</a>. Sometimes decisions need to be made over the objections of partisan opposition or of another branch of government. But the public can trust decision-makers only if those leaders check themselves. </p>

<p>Like many problems, political shamelessness may seem new, but thinkers stretching <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/reverence-9780199350803?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;#">back to the ancient Greeks</a> have warned of its perils, which they described as “irreverence” – the failure to respect something bigger than ourselves. If today’s politics seem threatened by some such menace, it may be because we are neglecting this ancient wisdom. </p>

<h2>Awaken to our ignorance</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most searching account of this problem and what to do about it can be found in a work by <a href="https://thegreatthinkers.org/plato/biography/">the Greek philosopher Plato</a>, who died in 347 B.C.E. The text is known simply as the “<a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Laws_of_Plato/ds7aF6Am0OsC?hl=en&amp;gbpv=0">Laws</a>.”</p>

<p>Like his better-known “<a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Republic_of_Plato/_6Y7DAAAQBAJ?hl=en&amp;gbpv=0">Republic</a>,” the “Laws” envisions a “city in speech”: a utopia, a place that exists only in theory. But whereas the city of the “Republic” is ruled autocratically by “philosopher kings,” the “Laws” explores the possibilities and limitations of what is now called constitutional government. </p>

<p>All of Plato’s writings suggest that the most significant political fact is the scarcity of wisdom: the dearth of knowledge needed to live a flourishing human life. What’s more, he taught, most of us don’t recognize our own ignorance – indeed, we powerfully resist recognizing it. </p>

<p>Plato’s “Laws” examines the rule of law in light of this fact. It teaches that the function of law is to awaken citizens and politicians to their own ignorance and then to point them to a wise, ethical authority. </p>

<p>At its best, law wouldn’t just protect security or individual rights. It would provoke people to recognize their profound need of a standard of good and bad beyond their own judgment. </p>

<p>Otherwise, human nature being what it is, Plato saw that each person would corruptly “honor his own” – himself and everything connected to him – “<a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Laws_of_Plato/ds7aF6Am0OsC?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1&amp;pg=PA118&amp;printsec=frontcover">more than the truth</a>.” He would rationalize his own prejudices and justify his own selfishness.</p>

<h2>Reverence as a virtue</h2>

<p>In the “Laws,” the antidote to this problem <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Laws_of_Plato/ds7aF6Am0OsC?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1">is what Plato calls “aidos</a>,” or reverence: the virtue governing shame, as well as awe. Taken by themselves, shame and awe are neither laudable nor blameworthy. But to have reverence, Plato suggests, is to feel these emotions for the right reasons. </p>

<p>Shame and awe go together for Plato because they both involve a feeling of diminishment: a sense of our own limits. With shame, this feeling is social, connected to the fear of someone else’s disapproving gaze. With awe, the feeling of smallness is inspired by something that makes our own concerns and capacities seem trivial – something like God or the divine.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man seen in silhouette sits atop a large rock looking out over the ocean on a gray day." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765342/original/file-20261010-50-8fdr4f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>It might seem as though a virtuous person would not feel shame; she would simply never do or say anything shameful. But in Plato’s eyes, precious few achieve so pure a virtue. For most, fear of shame is a necessary backstop to push people away from what wrongly tempts them. Likewise, awe prevents people from underestimating difficult tasks or from overestimating themselves. </p>

<p>According to the “Laws,” the proper object of reverence is wisdom, represented as God: “<a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Laws_of_Plato/ds7aF6Am0OsC?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1">the measure of all things</a>.” The text stresses the awesome nature of the wisdom needed to judge things well – the need to look for truth outside ourselves. It teaches that we should be ashamed to “measure” things by reference only to our own fallible judgment.</p>

<h2>Awesome responsibility</h2>

<p>Reverence might seem irrelevant to modern politics. In liberal democracies, public life is devoted to securing liberty, not to learning virtue. Shaming people for disregarding the awesome nature of wisdom might appear a gross violation of their freedom of conscience. Modern societies can scarcely agree on what is shameful to begin with.</p>

<p>Reverence might also seem to involve a piety that is out of place in a diverse democracy. Many people believe in God, but political decisions are judged by secular standards like their popularity, or by whether they benefit the public interest. </p>

<p>Nevertheless, I would argue that modern politics continue to depend on something akin to reverence. Liberal democracies might not use government to teach virtue directly, but they do need citizens and statesmen who appreciate the limits of their own judgment and their need of higher principles to guide their decisions.  </p>

<p>It helps that awe need not be inspired by gods – or wisdom, which was what Plato truly revered. Citizens might feel awe, for example, at the enormous responsibility of self-government. As philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote in the 18th century, <a href="https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/cole-the-social-contract-and-discourses#lf0132_label_101">democracy is more suited to gods than men</a>: rightly understood, it is demanding in the highest degree. </p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=vote%20line%20u.s.&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Nic Antaya</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Modern liberty is especially demanding; it isn’t only a matter of having a right to vote or speak our minds, as important as such rights may be. It is also a matter of having to choose between myriad ethical, religious and cultural traditions, or to choose none at all. </p>

<p>Such freedom is both a boon and a burden. In today’s democracies, citizens are responsible for their own ethical lives: for determining what should count as right and wrong, good and bad. </p>

<p>But it is precisely because we are free to waste our freedom, Plato might say, that we need reverence all the more: feeling awe for the responsibility of using that freedom well, and shame when we do not. As for political leaders, until they cease to find an approving audience for their contempt of principled behavior, the shamelessness that many observers find so disturbing will likely continue.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288318/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: President Donald Trump and US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in the White House on March 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, is out of a job after serious corruption allegations.  What happened? Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after being shown the door earlier in the day by Trump’s brand-new White House press secretary, who announced at a briefing that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.  Her departure comes just six days after a bombshell Wall Street Journal story , which described Guilfoyle’s efforts to solicit money from a Trump donor, including $100,000 to pay down a credit card bill, in exchange for access to Trump officials and conservative media figures.  Guilfoyle also attempted to conceal those efforts: In one text to the donor, Eric Deters, she wrote, “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.” Who is Guilfoyle? Fallen MAGA royalty
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, is also the ex-fiancée of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. (and, more distantly, the ex-wife of current California Gov
There appears to be little love lost between Guilfoyle and Trump, however
On Tuesday, he told reporters that Guilfoyle “wasn’t a member of my family

She I guess dated my son a long time ago.” (The Don Jr.-Guilfoyle relationship is thought to have ended in 2024.) Why was she forced out? Corruption allegations are not, generally speaking, dealbreakers in Trumpworld; the president and his children are all innovators when it comes to profiting off the presidency , and there’s plenty of self-dealing going on around them
That being said, Guilfoyle may have crossed the line in two specific ways: one, her alleged corruption benefited her and not the Trump family
And two, the allegations are embarrassingly unsubtle even by the standards of the second Trump administration
The combination appears to have been too much

And with that, it’s time to log off… This New York Times story , about what a potential superhabitable world elsewhere in the cosmos could look like, was a very cool, very sci-fi read — and we may find out more about the existence of such planets soon, with new space telescopes planned for next year and beyond.  You can read the full story here with a gift link
Enjoy, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!
