body: On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring the Bureau of Prisons to “ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Issued alongside a record 26 other orders that day, it was an unsurprising development, because Trump had made this issue one of the centerpieces of his 2024 campaign
The fate of that executive order, as well as the US Bureau of Prisons’ (“BOP”) memoranda implementing the order, is now before the Supreme Court in a case called Trump v

And, while this case obviously has high stakes for incarcerated transgender people specifically, the Court’s resolution of this case could potentially have far greater reach — cutting off many cis and transgender people’s access to healthcare while they are incarcerated
That’s because one of the central questions in Kingdom — though this issue is not yet before the justices — is when the Constitution requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people

Gamble (1976), the Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments” imposes on the government an “obligation to provide medical care for those whom it is punishing by incarceration.” People in prison, after all, cannot simply drive themselves to the hospital if they get sick
If the prison does not give them adequate medical care, they will suffer untreated and potentially die
For procedural reasons, the Court is unlikely to opine on whether Estelle requires prisons to provide gender-affirming care to trans people right away

But the question of when the Eighth Amendment requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people is front and center in the Kingdom case , which means the Court could potentially use Kingdom to limit all imprisoned people’s access to healthcare — or even to undercut the Constitution’s protections against cruel and unusual punishments more broadly
Ironically, this case also arises out of a famous political blunder by pro-trans advocates

Kamala Harris was seeking her party’s 2020 presidential nomination, the ACLU circulated a questionnaire to candidates that asked if they would use presidential authority “to ensure that transgender and nonbinary people who rely on the state for medical care — including those in prison and immigration detention — will have access to comprehensive treatment associated with gender transition, including all necessary surgical care?”  Harris responded that she would, and also said that she “pushed the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation to provide gender transition surgery to state inmates” while she was state attorney general.  Years later, during his 2024 debate with Harris, Trump claimed that the then-vice president “ wants to do transgender operations on illegal aliens that are in prison .” And not long after, his opposition to gender-affirming care for trans people in prison became a key part of his campaign
It’s unclear why the ACLU thought it was a good idea to shine a light on this issue in 2019 because, at the time, the BOP provided gender-affirming care to people in federal prison

The ACLU — which represents the pro-trans side in the Kingdom case — now argues that transgender people in federal prison have had access to at least some forms of gender-affirming care “ since at least 1992 .” Indeed, Trump’s own administration concluded in a 2018 memo that the Bureau of Prisons’ “statutory mandate to provide basic medical and mental health care” to incarcerated people obligated it to provide “pharmaceutical interventions (e.g., cross-gender hormone therapy), hair removal and surgery (if individualized assessment indicates surgical intervention is applicable)” to transgender people in prison if their doctors determined that these interventions are “medically necessary care.” In any event, regardless of why Trump fixated on cutting off trans healthcare for people in federal prison, Kingdom is now before the Court

That means that the fate of trans people in prison — and, if the Eighth Amendment issue eventually reaches the Court, all incarcerated people — is now in the hands of a Republican Court that is often hostile to trans litigants, and that has, at times, signaled that it wants to drastically roll back the scope of the Eighth Amendment
What are the legal issues in the Kingdom case? At least since Estelle , the Court has held that people who are incarcerated are not also sentenced to live and die without medical care

Plata (2011), “a prison that deprives prisoners of basic sustenance, including adequate medical care, is incompatible with the concept of human dignity and has no place in civilized society.” Under Estelle and Brown , transgender people often have a right to gender-affirming care during their incarceration
As the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held in Edmo v
Corizon (2019), such a person must show that they have a “serious medical need” for such care — typically by demonstrating that the care was prescribed to them by their health provider
But the Constitution does not permit prisons to deny medically necessary care to incarcerated people
In Kingdom , the ACLU raised this Eighth Amendment argument in the lower courts, but those lower courts ruled in favor of transgender people in prison on different, much more technical legal grounds

For over three decades, from at least 1992 to 2025, according to the ACLU’s brief to the justices , the BOP provided at least some gender-affirming care, including hormone therapy, to transgender people

This matters because, when a federal agency changes its policies, a federal law typically requires it to “ examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action , including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.” This explanation often must explain the agency’s justification for “disregarding facts and circumstances” that justified the previous policy

Both the ACLU and the lower courts that heard Kingdom argue that the Trump administration did not comply with this obligation when it cut off care for trans people in prison.  Among other things, the district court that heard this case determined that the administration cited “ zero evidence from its own medical or mental health care professionals to support its conclusions” against providing transgender healthcare

While the Trump administration argues that providing gender-affirming care makes prisons less safe, the district court also noted that “the government has not cited a single instance of gender-affirming care giving rise to safety concerns despite having provided such care for many years.” Is this a persuasive legal argument against the Trump administration’s new policy? I think it is
And so did three federal judges that previously heard the Kingdom case

But the fate of trans people in prison is now in the hands of a Supreme Court that rarely rules in favor of transgender litigants, and that has a history of handing down legally incoherent opinions that are inconsistent with the Court’s own precedents , and that also deny legal rights to trans people

The current Court’s uncertain commitment to the Eighth Amendment Because the lower courts that heard Kingdom did not rule on the Eighth Amendment question, Kingdom should not currently give the justices an opportunity to roll back Estelle

But, in the likely event that this Court rejects the ACLU’s argument that the Trump administration did not adequately explain its new policy, the case will return to the lower courts and the Eighth Amendment issue will be fully litigated — teeing up the Eighth Amendment question for the justices to decide in the near future

This issue could arise, moreover, at the exact moment that some justices are pushing for sweeping changes to how their Court understands the term “cruel and unusual punishments.” Indeed, at least some of the Supreme Court’s recent Eighth Amendment precedents suggest that the Republican justices want a wholesale rewrite of the Court’s previous precedents laying out what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment

Since the mid-to-late twentieth century, the Court has held that, in Chief Justice Earl Warren’s words, the Eighth Amendment “must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society .” Thus, as certain forms of punishment grow more uncommon, they become more constitutionally dubious
This “evolving standards of decency” framework is front and center in nearly every major Supreme Court decision interpreting the Eighth Amendment for the last five or six decades, including Estelle
Precythe (2019), however, the Court’s Republican majority seemed to abandon this framework

Although decades worth of pre -Bucklew decisions established that a punishment is unconstitutional if it is considered cruel and unusual today , Bucklew suggested that a method of punishment is unconstitutional only if it “had fallen out of use” at “the time of the founding.”  Bucklew did list some methods of punishment that fail this test, but they are things like “disemboweling” or “burning alive.”    Thus, if taken seriously, Bucklew ’s new approach to Eighth Amendment cases would dramatically expand the government’s power to impose harsh punishments

The late Justice Antonin Scalia, for example, argued that a Bucklew -like approach to the Eighth Amendment does not prohibit the government from executing most intellectually disabled offenders, and that it does not limit the government’s ability to impose excessive punishments for minor crimes
In fairness, some of the Court’s post- Bucklew decisions are inconsistent with the framework the Court laid out in that case
So at least some of the justices who joined Bucklew may have since decided that it’s a bad idea to toss out the Court’s entire framework for Eighth Amendment cases
But Bucklew was one hell of a warning shot over the bow of the Eighth Amendment
And the mere fact that the Bucklew decision exists means that advocates for humane punishments must hold their breath any time this Court is asked whether a particular punishment is cruel and unusual
In the worst-case scenario for people in prison, a case like Kingdom could inspire the Republican justices to overrule — or, at least, drastically limit — decisions like Estelle and Brown
That would mean that all incarcerated people, regardless of their gender identity, could lose access to medically necessary care unless the government decides to give it to them as an act of grace.

title: Trump’s revenge campaign comes for Ilhan Omar
excerpt: Homeland Security Investigations outside the home of Rep
body: Homeland Security Investigations outside the home of Rep

Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. | Andrew Leyden/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Or…something like that! On Tuesday morning, Minnesota Rep
Ilhan Omar launched a fundraising drive in response to the Trump administration’s unusual predawn raid of her Washington, DC, residence
The raid, which went down Monday, is reportedly part of a criminal investigation into Omar’s immigration history
The Democratic Congress member was born in Somalia and came to the US as a child, becoming a naturalized citizen in 2000 at age 17

Omar has since become one of the most prominent progressive voices in Congress and a regular thorn in the side of President Donald Trump, who on Monday called her “terrible” and “totally crooked.” Vice President JD Vance has similarly claimed , without evidence, that Omar “committed immigration fraud.” On Monday, the New York Post reported that the investigation may have sprung from mistakes Omar’s late father made while filling out her citizenship application roughly 30 years ago.  Needless to say, decades-old citizenship paperwork is not the kind of threat to public safety that typically commands the resources of the Department of Homeland Security’s investigations branch. ( That same branch is charged with investigating transnational gangs and terrorists.) And the raid is unusual for another reason, too: By longstanding practice , the Justice Department avoids taking any public steps in investigations involving political candidates within 60 days of an election
The midterms are just three weeks from now.  This investigation is unlikely to affect Omar in the midterms, however

In the words of her longshot Republican challenger, John Nagel, Minnesota’s Fifth District is among “ the ‘bluest’…in the country .” The raid may have even galvanized Omar’s supporters, dozens of whom rallied at a Minneapolis park on Monday afternoon

Some held banners that read “we stand with Ilhan.” Another sign read, simply, “see you at the polls.” Go a little deeper View Link Omar now belongs to an unenviable and surprisingly populous club: political opponents of Trump whom his administration has threatened with criminal indictments and investigations.  I initially planned to list them out for you here, but then realized that list would be perilously long

By my back-of-the-envelope count, there are at least 30 Democratic politicians, public officials, and Trump-world defectors who have been accused of, investigated for, or charged with crimes during the second Trump administration.  It’s easy to forget the scale of that campaign , however, because many of these efforts have (thus far!) stalled out or collapsed
In several cases , the administration opened much-publicized and thinly supported investigations that have yet to yield charges. (See, for instance, the criminal probe into writer E
Andrew Cuomo .)  In at least two cases — that of then-Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell and several Minnesota officials — federal judges tossed out subpoenas for lack of evidence
And in one high-profile instance earlier this year, a grand jury refused to indict six Democratic members of Congress who released a video reminding soldiers to refuse illegal orders

The legal bar for issuing such an indictment is actually pretty low — which makes this grand jury’s refusal a telling rebuke of the administration.  But these judicial setbacks aren’t exactly reason for optimism
The federal court system is becoming increasingly partisan, and as long as Republicans hold the Senate, they’ll be able to stack it with ever-more conservative and deferential judges

And several of the most partisan judges already on the bench are “openly auditioning” for Supreme Court slots, as my colleague Ian Millhiser recently put it .  In other words, in the not-so-distant future, the court system may provide a weaker check on presidential overreach
And that’s bad news not only for the Ilhan Omars of the world…but also for American democracy.  One link for later ➨ Turn off your sleep tracker

If your sleep hygiene and underlying health are both good, but you still struggle to catch enough ZZs, then you might actually want to tone down your quest for better sleep . “What you see in people with insomnia is that they’re trying too hard,” one sleep scientist told Vox
Analyzing your sleep scores and timing your naps can create anxiety that further fuels insomnia.  Before you go… Did you know… that Coke, Pepsi, and Dr
Pepper were all invented by 19th-century pharmacists ? At the time, it was widely believed that carbonated water could cure illnesses

And sugary syrups made said water vastly more delicious.  Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the 2025 Pixar film set in the “Communiverse”? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the three-letter successor of tube TVs
That would be LCD, which stands for liquid crystal display.

title: Florida’s uniquely horrifying death penalty system
excerpt: The execution chamber in the Texas State Penitentiary at Huntsville in 1984. | Jerry Cabluck/Sygma via Getty Images Late last month, the state of Tennessee atte
body: The execution chamber in the Texas State Penitentiary at Huntsville in 1984. | Jerry Cabluck/Sygma via Getty Images Late last month, the state of Tennessee attempted to execute Christa Pike, a woman who has been on death row for decades after killing a classmate as a teenager.  The execution failed: Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, making her the first person ever to do so
The botched execution comes at a strange moment for capital punishment in America
Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades
And for a long time, the number of executions was falling, too
But since 2021, executions have been increasing again
The recent surge has been driven largely by one state: Florida

According to Pamela Colloff , who covers the criminal justice system for ProPublica and wrote about Florida’s use of the death penalty for New York Times Magazine this summer, 40 percent of the executions conducted in the US last year were in Florida. “There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida,” Colloff explained on a recent episode of Vox’s The Gray Area podcast. “Among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is.” I spoke with Colloff earlier this month following Pike’s failed execution about what happened in Tennessee, what’s driving Florida’s recent zeal for executions, and why victims’ families are often unsatisfied by the death penalty process
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to The Gray Area wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify . (This interview also appeared more recently on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast.) We’re taping shortly after news came out that a woman in Tennessee who was on death row, authorities attempted to put her to death

They gave her two doses of lethal injection medication, and she survived.  How much of the decline in the use of the death penalty has to do with, in your estimation, people feeling like there’s no way to do it that’s humane?  This is the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, just to give you a sense of things
This is more common there than in other states
They’ve changed their drug protocols and we don’t know a lot about what went wrong with Christa Pike

In May, it was an issue with accessing veins , which can be an issue with lethal injection.  I think it’s also important for people to remember that we had the electric chair as the method of execution through the ’80s and into the ’90s in some places

While [lethal injection] is considered a far more humane, quote-unquote, way to do this, we can see that nothing is perfect.  I will say that while the issues of botched executions are very important, and I think there are some other ones coming up to be concerned about, I am more interested in how it is that other errors are made, that other people end up with the ultimate punishment when that perhaps was not the right punishment for what occurred

You’ve also written that death penalty convictions are just expensive, right? And on top of that, DNA evidence has made it clear that many of the people who were being convicted were not guilty, or there wasn’t strong enough evidence to convict them

How do you think about that mix of factors? Florida, which I’ve spent a lot of time writing about, is the leading place in America by a mile in terms of the number of executions, and has a very large death row
Florida’s also the leader in wrongful death row convictions
Just to give you a sense of things, Florida holds the distinction of 30 death row exonerations
What that means is in the modern era — the past roughly 50 years — there have been 30 men who were given dates of execution who now walk free

And for anyone who pays any attention to how the criminal justice system works and how incredibly difficult it is to overturn a wrongful conviction, if we have 30 people in Florida who have that distinction, we know that there are many more
What’s going on in Florida? When did you realize that something was different there? It really ramped up last year
Last year, Florida executed 40 percent of the people who were executed in the US in the last calendar year

In this year, there have been 16 men who’ve been executed in Florida so far.  Just to give you a comparison, Texas is the next state with the highest number of executions, and they’ve executed six men in that time
We already have outlier states, primarily southern states, and then we have Florida being the ultimate outlier
There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida

The thing that fascinated me the most is, among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is
I went back and looked at what were the patterns here, what were the things guiding Gov
DeSantis’s thinking in setting these dates, and was fascinated to see and very troubled to see that there are a number of men who’ve been there so long
These are men who were convicted when Gerald Ford was president, just to make this real to people
But the dates are not being set among the men who are what are called death-eligible, meaning that they’ve gone through all their appeals
They aren’t being done chronologically
There’s no rhyme or reason to the process
And so there’s this speculation game among victims’ families, prisoners, their advocates about who will be next
And men can sit there on death row for decades with that hanging over them, and that is a Florida phenomenon

You wrote about Florida’s death row turning from something like a purgatory where people stay for a long time into something closer to an assembly line, right? I was so struck by the fact that in Florida, in order to have this pace of executions, there were people who were receiving their dates 30 days, sometimes fewer, from their execution dates.  Just to give people a sense of why that is unusual, there are so many things that kick into gear when a death warrant is written
There are numerous legal maneuvers and next steps that happen in the courts

To give you a quick example, there was one defendant in Florida this spring who, five days before he was scheduled to be executed, was finally granted the ability to test DNA evidence in his case that had gone untested
He had great lawyers who didn’t sleep to make that happen, but that it came as close as five days to his execution date
I think that should give us all pause about how fast this is moving.  You have multiple people in the queue at the same time
There’s a place — a different unit than Florida’s death row — that you’re taken to once you get your date, called death watch

title: How housing victories in San Diego, Austin, and Atlanta could spread nationwide
excerpt: Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens has helped advance the city’s broader effort to build or preserve 20,000 affordable homes by 2030. | Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via
body: Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens has helped advance the city’s broader effort to build or preserve 20,000 affordable homes by 2030. | Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images As rents and homelessness climbed in San Diego over the last decade, leaders watched in frustration as affordable housing projects took months to get approved

The longer a project dragged on, the more expensive it became.   Housing in America is notoriously slow and complicated to build, so San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria decided to use one lever he had available
In January 2023, he signed an executive order to speed up project approvals , so every fully affordable project now had to be reviewed in 30 business days or less
To meet this new goal, San Diego had to overhaul how it had been handling permitting
The city streamlined work that had been spread across multiple departments and filled positions it had budgeted for but left vacant
Within a year, fully affordable projects were clearing review in nine days on average
Citywide, 2023 marked San Diego’s biggest year for housing permits since at least 2005, with 9,691 homes approved, or an 82 percent jump from the year before
Key takeaways Bloomberg Philanthropies is funding up to 30 cities to copy housing fixes that worked in San Diego, Austin, and Atlanta
The bet is that cities lack the know-how to execute good ideas, not the ideas themselves
It’s not clear what will happen to city capacity when the foundation funding runs out
Austin, Texas embraced a different approach to tackling its housing shortage
After years of local zoning reform, the city legalized up to three homes on most single-family lots in late 2023, then cut the minimum lot size from 5,750 square feet to 1,800 in 2024
Those changes made it easier to add homes, including backyard accessory dwelling units (ADUs), and followed a broader construction boom that has helped bring rents down
Austin, which was becoming increasingly unaffordable, is now one of the few major American cities where asking rents have fallen since the pandemic
Atlanta adopted a third housing strategy that didn’t require changing any laws at all

Mayor Andre Dickens rallied the heads of every public agency that affects housing, from the city’s housing authority and school system to the transit agency and land bank, and convened them in one room on a regular basis
He called it a “housing strike force” and it has helped advance the city’s broader effort to build or preserve 20,000 affordable homes by 2030

Every housing deal now comes to the mayor’s office, Dickens told me, and “I just start pushing buttons to push them out the door.”  Seen as a nationwide issue, the housing shortage is an enormously difficult problem, sitting at the nexus of the economy, the financial system, and decades of local zoning decisions
But the fixes don’t all have to be complex
A mayor can do all three of these — faster permitting, ADUs, a housing strike team — without waiting on Congress or their state legislature to act
And now one major nonprofit is betting that other cities could adopt them too
On Tuesday, Bloomberg Philanthropies is announcing that it will fund up to 30 cities to adopt one of those three housing ideas
Each will get between $450,000 and $750,000 directly and two years of help from Accelerator for America and the digital consultancy Public Digital, also funded by Bloomberg
The philanthropy has already selected the first 15 cities, including Albuquerque, Chattanooga, Cleveland, Durham, Louisville, Miami, Nashville, Pittsburgh, and San Jose
By housing construction standards, the money doesn’t go very far

The grants are geared toward hiring city staff, buying new software, and helping cities quickly develop the expertise that let San Diego, Austin, and Atlanta do what they did. “You don’t need everyone to be innovating everything all the time when there are good ideas in the world that are working,” said James Anderson, who leads Bloomberg Philanthropies’ government innovation program. “They need help adapting those ideas to local contexts.” According to Anderson, the cities were chosen because their mayors had already taken hard political votes on zoning, and wanted help now to do more

On the federal level, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law in July, and it creates competitive grants for cities that modernize their permitting, for preapproved housing plans, and that open up their public land
These are the same reforms Bloomberg is now funding, and cities that can show they’ve already done work around it will be better positioned to tap into new federal dollars

Mayors say they’ve seen big federal programs pass before and then found that actually leveraging those new funding streams in practice can be quite difficult. “We saw that with the Inflation Reduction Act,” Cleveland Mayor Justin Bibb told me. “Even some of the aspects of the bipartisan infrastructure bill, there was a lot of red tape to get some of that stuff across the finish line.” The Bloomberg bet is that figuring out what to do isn’t as hard as organizing the knowledge of how to do it
The philanthropy thinks that with enough money and hand-holding, good ideas can spread
It’s an experiment worth testing, but even at the outset there are real limits to what kind of help a short-term infusion of cash can do in practice
San Diego, Austin, and Atlanta all had substantial housing staff in place before they started, and many cities don’t have the same depth to draw on
A two-year grant covers a few staff roles, but doesn’t guarantee they’ll stay long-term in a city where most of the local budget is already committed
What a “housing strike force” actually is Dickens had campaigned for office in Atlanta on building 20,000 affordable units in eight years

When he became mayor in 2022, his staff told him the city was on pace to fall 4,000 to 5,000 units short of this goal, and that the main federal subsidy for affordable housing, which gets rationed out by the state in fixed amounts each year, wasn’t going to make up the difference
What Atlanta did have was land, spread across more than a dozen public entities, each with its own board and its own ideas about what the land was for

One 10-acre city site just northwest of downtown was being used to store trash cans before delivery to residents. “It’s not the highest and best use of the land, but we’ve been doing it for decades,” Josh Humphries, then Dickens’ senior housing adviser, told The Guardian
So Dickens pulled the heads of those agencies into one body reporting through his chief housing officer

The transit system and school district both answer to their own boards, so his pitch was that they weren’t giving anything up by getting involved. “You are still in charge of your organization, these are your deals, but we are an accelerator,” Dickens told me

They spent nothing setting it up and hired no new staff for the strike force itself — though when Dickens advises other mayors, he’s blunter about the pressure a mayor would need to exert in convening such a team

title: Maybe secular liberals can’t save democracy
excerpt: A priest speaks to parishioners during Sunday Catholic Mass inside the Our Lady of Guadalupe Church on August 10, 2025, in Mission, Texas. | Tom Brenner for the
body: A priest speaks to parishioners during Sunday Catholic Mass inside the Our Lady of Guadalupe Church on August 10, 2025, in Mission, Texas. | Tom Brenner for the Washington Post via Getty Images To the average observer concerned with the future of American democracy, it might be easy to conclude that religion has been part of the problem — particularly over the last few years

Right-wing religious leaders, including the leading Southern Baptist televangelist Robert Jeffress, have endorsed “ Christian nationalism ”; other evangelical pastors and conservative Catholic intellectuals have been openly pondering if America should become more of a theocracy; Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who once called for an “ American crusade ,” evoking bloody medieval religious campaigns, has referenced Christian theology in statements about the Iran war

To critics, these examples show that American religion is becoming an active threat to pluralism and tolerance — the ideas that make American democracy work.  But what if the solution to this anti-democratic slide is also religion — more religion than the US currently has? Key takeaways The authors of a new book argue that declining levels of religiosity have worsened polarization, which has led to a backslide in democracy
To reverse this trend, the authors suggest everyone, but particularly liberals and secular people, engage with religion more and take lessons on debate and disagreement from faith traditions

For those who do identify as religious already, this would mean participating in organized religion; for those who are not religious, this would mean approaching religion and religious people with more openness and curiosity
This argument has limitations, but there are signs it is becoming more widespread, including the rise of religious Democrats and the pope’s recent comments

A new book by two thinkers from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum argues that declining levels of religiosity across the board, but particularly among liberals, have deepened political polarization, which in turn has corroded democratic norms

Now, they argue, one of the most effective ways for liberals to stand up for democracy is to engage with religious communities and their scriptural traditions with more respect, openness, and curiosity
The authors also urge liberals who are believers themselves to embrace organized religion and return to it themselves

Conservative evangelical Christian Matthew Kaemingk and liberal Muslim writer Shadi Hamid argue in Can Religion Save Democracy? that there’s a necessary and unique role that religious institutions and organized religion must play in American public life
Religion serves a fundamental regulating purpose, tempering emotions, fundamentalism, and nihilism
And when that fades away, those base instincts and emotions get channeled into our politics
They write: As Americans exit churches in droves, they’re not leaving behind their religious passions
Instead, they’re transferring those passions to the political battlefield

In this new post-religious context, Christian faith and Scripture function less as moral constraints within evangelical circles and more as political cudgels to use against one’s opponents. “We’re not trying to convert [nonbelievers],” Hamid told me in an interview. “Believing is one thing, but believing that religion can play a positive role is another

And we want to encourage secular readers to embrace the second proposition, even if they don’t believe religion is true or don’t believe God exists.” What happens when religion recedes from the public square At the core of Kaemingk and Hamid’s argument is a simple case: There is an innate religion-shaped hole in people in the 21st century, which has been slowly replaced with politics, unbridled passions, and secular ideologies

The loss of religion hasn’t meant a loss of religious convictions, but instead has meant the rise of a new fanaticism, either secular or fundamentalist, while depriving everyone of the good things that organized and institutional religion can do
It’s not a completely novel argument; it’s a combination of St

Augustine’s famous line that “our hearts are restless until they rest in [God]” and of the political scientist Robert Putnam’s modern case that churches and religious communities provided the third spaces that fostered civic partnership, trust, meaning, and belonging.  But they also connect these lines of thinking to what the Dutch philosopher Abraham Kuyper used to argue around the turn of the 19th century: that all people are religious, and that something very similar to religious fervor quietly powers all political movements

Religion is “pervasive, public, and pluriform” — an essential part of being human, whose absence leaves nihilism, fear, and distrust in isolated, but still fanatical, individuals. “If Kuyper is correct that all human beings desire ultimate belief and belonging, then erasing or sequestering religion won’t extinguish our spiritual passions
They will simply shift elsewhere,” Kaemingk and Hamid write

And that shift has been toward politics, candidates, elections, and secular “creeds” that provide identity, belonging, moral certainty, and salvific promises without the accountability, guidance, and caution that religious traditions can provide
It’s not hard to find examples of what Kaemingk and Hamid mean here
From 2016 to 2024, many observed elements of quasi-religious fervor in movements powering Trump and Woke 1.0

Trump’s strongman appeal generated a cult of personality around him, while anti-Trump resistance efforts and progressive social movements often took on qualities people also found quasi-religious: in-group markers, language, and customs, BlueAnon theories
What’s left is a stalemate, with more conservative religious believers bunched up on one end, and nonreligious but equally passionate citizens on the other end

Kaemingk and Hamid argue that people on the left often respond by denigrating religion and religious people, dismissing those who try to defend or practice it in the public square, or forcing them to adopt secular language and thinking instead of letting religious people bring their full selves to the public space

But the way out of this current stalemate, Kaemingk and Hamid suggest, is for people on the left to be open, curious, and respectful with the devoutly faithful, whether they’re neighbors or candidates running for office.  “For that audience, my desire is to say, ‘Hey, you don’t have to believe in religion, but you can recognize the positive aspects of religion,’” Hamid told me
That involves practical, daily activities and more high-minded appeals
In regular life, the authors recommend prayer, or prayer-like practices for nonbelievers, to help better understand and forgive opponents

They suggest there can be benefits for both nonreligious and religious people to meditate on scriptural and theological teachings about forgiveness, debate, disagreement, salvation, and why earthly politics shouldn’t be taken so seriously.  And they urge liberals in particular to reengage with religious communities and congregations

Religious liberals should avoid isolation or solitary, individualized faith, the authors recommend, and instead return to congregations and specific churches or places of worship to become part of a community and find purpose

For nonreligious liberals, Kaemingk and Hamid suggest they reexamine their own ideological priorities and be open to the possibility of being wrong on some of them, and potentially engage with organized religion to better understand a religious worldview

Kaemingk and Hamid offer a specific challenge for liberals and secular Americans that might seem a bit unsavory: They have to realize that they are not blameless for the polarization and radical religious fervor that exists right now through their dismissal of organized religion

Their earlier denigration of organized religion around the turn of this century (think of the New Atheist movement), combined with many leaving institutional churches or failing to participate in religious life, has all contributed to the capture of these institutions by unsavory political opponents, or helped in the decline of more moderate congregations
And any attempt to stop this continued slide away from pluralistic democracy hinges on a collective effort between religious and nonreligious Americans to reverse these trends

This argument has its limitations Here’s an obvious question: If religion is so good at moderating people, why hasn’t it been able to temper emotions among the religious already? The most loyal Republican voters over the past few cycles have tended to be evangelical and nondenominational Christians, followed by white Catholics — both of which tend to report above-average levels of religious participation

They’ve stuck with Trump and the GOP over the last decade, which has been defined by polarization, authoritarian policies, and even moments of political violence, that both Kaemingk and Hamid say religion can fix.  Here’s an obvious question: If religion is so good at moderating people, why hasn’t it been able to temper emotions among the religious already? More generally, while there is evidence to suggest that evangelicals who leave their churches become more cynical and individualistic — a point in Kaemingk and Hamid’s favor — there’s not much evidence to suggest that the converse is true: that religious participation has actually tempered emotions, passions, and politics
Instead, there’s a case to be made, as the writer Robert P
Jones laid out recently , that the opposite seems to be true: The most religious folks tend to still be the most likely to support harsher Trump-era policies

title: What it would take to build a city on the moon
excerpt: You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu
body: You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu
Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags
Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies
And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp
There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars
The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new
But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements

If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water
Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation

But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition
China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon
And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms
What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go
Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system
The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos
The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general

And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical
It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher
SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done
A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings
It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain
For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue

And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales

Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán
Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp
In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F
Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids
And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.  Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher
NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold
Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant
But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe
On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night

But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle
Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings
Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely
Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions
It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions
The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe
Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night
Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious

title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
excerpt: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like c
body: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth
Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century
Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands

She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land
As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction
The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree

For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide
Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914

Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter

Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings
Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle

In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand

One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors

Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis
Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions

But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves
As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations
Rather than despair, she turned to restoration

Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land
Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says
But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies
Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary
In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow
In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow

In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees
Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases
In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root

These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015
She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests

Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun

Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed
Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades

Using data from Panama and Brazil, Dent published a follow-up in 2024 showing that plots with as little as 35% of tree cover can regenerate as forest.  “Having these long-term mapped forest plots is really valuable,” says Liza Comita, a professor of tropical forest ecology at Yale University, who is collaborating with Dent on projects that translate her findings into action. “It provides this really nice research infrastructure where you can build projects on top of that.”  In Panama, Dent works with nonprofits and carbon-crediting schemes to fast-track recovery
They’ve mapped corridors to reconnect forest fragments and made plans to reintroduce animals in “silent forests” that have lost much of their wildlife
They’re also working to replant tree species that can accelerate growth—what Comita calls assisted natural regeneration
Leaving plots alone may seem like the simpler option, but it can’t be done everywhere, says Dent
Many sites are too degraded.  Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which helps tree cover regain old-growth ­levels of richness
The two are working with the London-based carbon-crediting startup Ponterra to develop solutions for a region of southern Panama where remnant forests line the edges of abandoned ranches
Such sites almost always need some intervention, Comita explains
Many demand hands-on actions, such as enrichment planting.  Today, the questions projects like Ponterra are asking are closer to her own research, says Dent

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
excerpt: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane
body: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb
It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season

The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered
